Reference
The Town Plan

Before you startSoftware Architecture: The Town Plan#

A very short book for lead engineers who are asked to choose an architecture, say what the choice costs, write down why, and keep it true after they have left the room.

The promise

Read this in two evenings and you will be able to name the three qualities that decide a system's shape, analyse a trade-off in the open instead of by taste, recognise each of the common system-level styles and say what it is good and bad at, choose a style per system instead of per company, record the decision so that it outlives the people who made it, draw it so that others can read it, and keep it true with checks that run on every change.

It reads as one story. Bramble, an online shop, buys Quill, a wholesaler whose software is fifteen years old, works, and has almost none of its decisions written down. The failures in this book begin as decisions, even when they end as outages: one nobody can explain, one that cannot be made because nobody knows what matters, one made by fashion, one forgotten and argued three times, one silently reversed by a pull request that every reviewer approved. Each chapter opens with such a decision, the fix is the chapter's idea, and by the end of the chapter a new difficulty has appeared.

Every idea arrives four ways: a place in one running metaphor (a town and its buildings), a diagram of how it actually works, a one-sentence Remember it as line you can repeat out loud, and a dated account of who thought of it, when, and what they were reacting to. Every chapter then does what a mentor would do at a whiteboard: it names the traps and their tell-tale signs, gives you a small artefact with one planted flaw to find, and hands you three questions to ask whoever proposes the idea next, plus the one point on which experienced people still disagree, argued fairly from both sides.

Who this is for

You lead a team, or are about to. You have been asked "monolith or microservices?" as if those were the only two answers, and you have sat in a meeting where the same design decision was argued for the third time because nobody could find why it was made. You want the part of the field that lets you choose well, explain the cost and make the choice stick, without reading two thousand pages.

If you already run architecture reviews, write decision records as a habit and have fitness functions in your build, this book will be too slow for you; skim the At the whiteboard boxes, chapter 13's comparison table and the epilogue.

How to read it

  • Straight through the first time. Characteristics and trade-offs come before any style, because a style is only good relative to them; the styles run from one deployable to many, which is also the order of rising cost; choosing comes after you have met every candidate.
  • The boxes are where the book becomes a tool. The traps is a checklist. Spot it trains your eye; cover the answer. At the whiteboard is what to say in the meeting.
  • The style chapters (5 to 11) each answer the same five questions and draw the same five capabilities, so any two can be laid side by side.
  • The Epilogue is the reference: the metaphor table, the full review checklist, the style comparison table, two blank templates, the diagram legend, the timeline and a reading list by year.

The cast

Bramble sells stationery online and hosts marketplace sellers; it is built as a handful of services and one modular monolith, which is one deployable program whose internal borders are enforced. Quill sells office supplies to four thousand business accounts, each with its own contract prices, from one fifteen-year-old program and a batch that runs every night. Ana is head of architecture for both, and can no longer be in every room. Kofi is the staff engineer who measures things and remembers how they got that way. Ingrid has been Quill's architect for eleven years; she defends what works, and she knows why most of it is the way it is, though nobody ever asked her to write it down. Marcus is the consultant engaged to produce one target architecture for the merged company; his arguments for a single standard are the real ones, and when he is wrong it is because a premise fails here, not because he is foolish. Lena founded Bramble, bought Quill, and wants one company within a year.

Code, where it appears, is Java 21 and illustrates shape; it is not a buildable project. Artefacts (a scenario, a decision record) are shown in full, because the practice half of the book is about documents.

The sibling books

This is the third of three books about the same company, and each can be read alone. DDD and Microservices: The Atlas owns boundaries and integration: where to draw the borders inside a system, what the inside of one deployable looks like, and how services talk safely. System Design: The Depot owns data, scale and reliability: how to measure load, replicate, cache and stay up. This book owns styles, trade-offs and decisions. Where a chapter needs something a sibling owns, it gives one sentence and names the book and chapter.

Dates and sources

Every "who and when" in this book was checked against the primary source named in research/milestones.md in the book's repository, and the epilogue's reading list gives them by year. Where an idea has a famous date and a publication date that differ, the text uses the first public one and says so.

Chapter 1 · Act IThe Decision Nobody Remembered Making#

The problem

Six weeks after Bramble bought Quill, Lena asked for the first thing that would make them look like one company. A Bramble customer who also holds a Quill trade account should see their Quill contract price on Bramble's site. Kofi's team estimated two weeks: Quill's code has a pricing function, so call it from the product page.

It worked in test. In its first week live, a stationer in Leeds was quoted £41.20 for a case of copier paper on Bramble's site and invoiced £43.05 by Quill the next morning. Eleven more followed. The feature was switched off, twelve customers were refunded the difference, and two weeks became "we don't know".

Kofi found the cause in an afternoon. Quill does not work out a price when someone asks. Every night a batch recalculates every account's price for every product that account may buy, and writes the answers into one table of about nine million rows. Order entry reads the table. The spreadsheet upload reads the table. The invoices read the table. The function Kofi's team had called was a step from the middle of that batch, and at three in the afternoon it was reading supplier costs that had arrived since midnight and would not count until the next run.

Nothing on Quill's wiki said so. Ingrid knew. In her first year, eleven years ago, pricing an order as the customer typed it took eight seconds on the server they had, the suppliers sent their lists once a day, and the contracts promised that the morning's price would hold all day. So prices were fixed once a night. "Nobody asked," she said.

The idea

Architecture is the set of significant decisions about a system: the ones that are hard to change and expensive to get wrong. In the town this book is built in, architecture is the load-bearing walls, what is expensive to move once people live there. Design is the furniture, moved on a Saturday. "Prices are fixed once a night and read from a table" is a wall. Whether the table's key is a number or a string is furniture.

The two are ends of a spectrum, and there is one test for where a decision sits: what would it cost to reverse a year from now, and how many teams would have to agree?

Architecture Design
The question What is expensive to move? What is the best arrangement today?
At Quill Prices are fixed nightly; one database; one release for everything The name of the price table; which class rounds to the penny
To reverse it Months, several teams, customers notice A pull request
Who must agree Everyone who built on it The team that owns the code
If the reason is lost The next change breaks something far away Nothing much

Most people asked for a system's architecture describe its structure, the boxes and how they connect. That is one of four dimensions, as Richards and Ford list them. Structure is the style: Quill is a layered program and a nightly batch. Characteristics are what the system must be good at, which is chapter 2. Decisions are the rules that hold everywhere: prices are fixed nightly. Principles are guidelines rather than rules: prefer a batch step to a call between programs. The wall Kofi's team walked into was not in the structure. A diagram of Quill's boxes would not have shown it. It was a decision.

The diagram shows why the decision is architectural. Four parts of Quill were built on it over eleven years, each for a sensible local reason. The upload format has no price column because the table supplies one. Invoicing does not recheck a price because the table cannot have changed since the order. Move the wall and each of those is a change, a test and a conversation with customers.

Quill's wall was not a mistake. It was reasonable on the day. What went wrong is that it was never recognised as a wall, so it was never recorded, and that is accidental architecture: a house extended by every owner, with no drawings. Accidental does not mean bad. It means nobody can tell a wall from a partition without knocking on it, and Kofi's team knocked with a release.

An unrecorded decision has three costs, and Quill paid all of them in one week. Nobody could tell what was resting on it. Nobody could tell whether its reasons still held: on today's hardware an order prices in a few milliseconds, so the first reason has expired, while the supplier feed and the contracts have not changed. And the only copy of the reasons was one person, who was not asked because nobody knew there was a question.

The rule, then: write down the reason for anything that is hard to change. It has a limit. Recording every choice buries the walls among the furniture, and a team that writes a page for a variable name will stop reading its own pages. Record what fails the reversal test, and let the rest live in the code.

Remember it as: architecture is the walls you cannot move on a Saturday, and the reasons they were put there.

◷How we got hereDewayne Perry and Alexander Wolf gave the field its first widely used definition in 1992: architecture is…

Dewayne Perry and Alexander Wolf gave the field its first widely used definition in 1992: architecture is elements, form and rationale, and they borrowed the comparison with buildings on purpose. Rationale was the part industry dropped. Through the 1990s architecture came to mean a phase, and a thick document produced before coding by people who would not write the code. Martin Fowler's 2003 column "Who Needs an Architect?" reacted to that. He quoted Ralph Johnson: architecture is the shared understanding that the expert developers have of the system, the decisions you wish you could get right early, in short "the important stuff. Whatever that is". That moved the definition from a drawing to a property, how hard something is to change. The four dimensions in Richards and Ford (2020) are the same idea, itemised.

⚠The traps
  • Accidental architecture: the sign is a constraint everyone works around and nobody can date or explain, described as "it has always done that". Walls get built on walls, and the first person to move one finds out what was resting on it.
  • Architecture as a phase: the sign is an architecture document dated before the first commit and not edited since. Significant decisions go on being made after the phase ends; they just stop being noticed.
  • The framework mistaken for the architecture: the sign is the sentence "our architecture is Spring Boot, PostgreSQL and Kafka". That lists the building materials. Two systems made of the same three can have opposite shapes and fail in opposite ways.
◉Spot it

From a new team's wiki, on a page titled Architecture:

The returns service is a Java 21 application on the standard platform. It stores its data in PostgreSQL and publishes to the company message broker. It is built and deployed by the shared build system. Code follows the team style guide.

Show the answer

Answer Every sentence names a material or a tool and none records a decision: the page never says what the service must be good at, which choices would be expensive to reverse, or why they were made. The sign is that the page would be equally true of any other service in the company. The fix is to replace it with the three or four decisions that fail the reversal test, each with its reason, such as "refunds are issued only after the warehouse scans the parcel, because sellers dispute a fifth of returns".

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Which three decisions in this system would take more than a month to reverse, and where is each one written down?
  2. Who, by name, can explain why this constraint exists, and how many other people could?
  3. Is the original reason for this decision still true today, yes or no, and how do you know?

Still argued: how much architecture to decide before building. Kent Beck (1999) held that up-front design guesses at needs that have not arrived, and that the guesses are usually wrong. A team with good tests can let the design emerge by refactoring, deciding each thing when it is needed. George Fairbanks (2010) replied that some properties cannot be refactored in cheaply, among them security, the shape of the data and whether the system is distributed. The amount of early architecture should therefore be set by the size of the risk. Both accept that a wrong early decision is expensive. They differ on how many decisions are walls, and the working compromise is to decide early only what fails the reversal test, while admitting that you cannot always tell which decisions those are.

What Ana learned

  • Ask what a decision would cost to reverse before calling it design, and treat it as a wall when the answer is more than one team and one month.
  • Write the reason beside every wall, because the reason is what tells the next person whether the wall can come down.
  • Ask the person who has been there longest what the system assumes before promising a date for anything that touches it.

…but

Lena's reply was short: so move the wall and make pricing live. Ingrid asked three questions back. Live for whom? How quickly? And is the invoice still allowed to be right? Nobody in the room could say what Quill's system has to be good at. They only knew what it does.

Chapter 2 · Act IWhat Must This Building Survive?#

The problem

"Make pricing live" could not be decided, because nobody could say what would count as better. Lena brought in Marcus, the consultant who had advised Bramble before, to produce a target architecture for the merged company, and he began where a careful consultant begins: a workshop, with the standard quality model pinned up as a checklist, so that nothing would be overlooked.

By the end of the afternoon there were fourteen cards. Scalability, availability, security, performance, maintainability, portability and eight more, and every one had been voted high. Two teams took the cards away as their brief. Kofi's team spent a sprint putting a cache in front of the price table so that lookups would scale, for a system that takes three hundred orders an hour on its busiest day. The same team looks after the nightly batch, and that fortnight nobody was watching it grow: on a Monday it finished at 06:40. The warehouse opens at six. Forty people stood in it without pick lists, and the first lorries left late.

"The batch finishes before the warehouse opens" was on no card. Everyone at Quill knew it, so nobody had said it. Ingrid's own list was two items long: the invoice has to be right, and the run has to be done by six.

The idea

A system has things it does and things it must be good at. The second kind is called a quality attribute, or in the newer books an architecture characteristic; they are the same thing. In the town, a characteristic is what the building must survive: fire, crowds, floods, burglars. A hospital and a warehouse may have the same number of rooms. They are built differently because of what each must survive.

The two are often written in one list and confused:

Requirement Characteristic
Says What the system does How well, and under what conditions
At Quill An account gets its contract price A changed price is in force within five minutes
Lives in One feature The structure, across every feature
When it is wrong Fix the feature Change the architecture
Usually stated In writing, by whoever wants it Not at all, until it is missed

Some characteristics are explicit: Lena's "one company within a year" is a demand for systems that can be changed quickly. Many are implicit. Nobody writes "the invoice is right to the penny" because nobody imagines otherwise. The useful question for finding implicit ones is what would get someone phoned at home.

They come in three kinds. Operational characteristics are about how the system runs: availability, performance, scalability, recovery after a failure. Structural ones are about how it is built and changed: modularity, testability, how easily it deploys. Cross-cutting ones apply everywhere and belong to no part: security, auditability, what the law requires.

Marcus's cards failed because they ranked nothing. Each characteristic you design for costs structure, and they conflict. Every security check is a delay. Elasticity argues for many small parts and simplicity argues for one. At Quill, a price that changes within minutes pulls against an invoice that anyone can reproduce a year later. So an architecture is shaped by its driving characteristics: the three that decide the building, because nobody can afford all of them. Three is a rule of thumb with a limit. A regulator can hand you a fourth that you may not trade away, and then you have four, and you pay for it in a narrower choice of structures. Past that, every addition removes candidates until the only design left is one that does everything moderately.

Ana ran the session again with one question: if we could only be good at three things, which? Quill's answers were that an invoice can be reproduced to the penny, that the nightly run is finished by six even on a bad night, and, new since the acquisition, that a price can change during the day. Just as usefully, the session said what Quill is not designed for: sudden crowds and round-the-clock availability. Kofi's cache came out.

A named characteristic is still only a word. "Changeable pricing" can mean anything. A quality-attribute scenario makes it testable, in the way a fire officer does: "when the alarm sounds with 300 people inside, everyone is out in four minutes." It states a stimulus, the environment it arrives in, the response and a measure.

Written out as the document Ana's team keeps:

Scenario: a contract price changes during the day

Source: an account manager at Quill

Stimulus: changes one account's discount band

Environment: a normal trading day, about 300 orders an hour

Response: the next quote and the next order for that account use the new price, and the invoice shows the price that was quoted

Measure: in force within 5 minutes for 99 changes in 100; no invoice differs from its quote by a penny

The measure is what turns an opinion into a test. The environment matters as much: "within five minutes" during the nightly run is a different and much more expensive promise, and this scenario does not make it. How to take such measurements in a running system belongs to the system design book, The Depot, chapters 1 and 18.

Remember it as: name the three things the building must survive, and for each say what happens, under what conditions, and what number proves it.

◷How we got hereRequirements documents of the 1980s and 1990s ended with a section called "non-functional requirements", a…

Requirements documents of the 1980s and 1990s ended with a section called "non-functional requirements", a list of sentences such as "the system shall be fast and easy to maintain" that no test could fail. Len Bass, Paul Clements and Rick Kazman reacted to that in Software Architecture in Practice (1998): they argued that qualities, more than functions, decide a system's structure, and their second edition (2003) fixed the six-part form of the scenario so that a quality could be stated as something measurable. Standards bodies had been cataloguing the qualities themselves; ISO/IEC 25010 (2011, revised in 2023) is the list most checklists are copied from, eight characteristics each divided into several more, and it is the model Marcus pinned up. Richards and Ford (2020) renamed them architecture characteristics and added the advice Ingrid gave without having read it: choose few.

⚠The traps
  • Every characteristic a priority: the sign is a list of ten or more qualities all marked high, or the words "these are all non-negotiable". No trade can be made from such a list, so each team makes its own, differently.
  • The unmeasurable characteristic: the sign is an adjective with no number: "highly available", "fast", "scalable". It cannot fail a test, so it is met by declaration and discovered missing in production.
  • The forgotten implicit characteristic: the sign is a quality so obvious to the people who run the system that it is on no list, such as "finished before the warehouse opens". A new design breaks it on its first Monday.
  • The generic architecture: the sign is a design justified as "scalable, secure and resilient" that would suit any company equally. It was derived from no particular driver, so it serves the one thing this business cannot do without no better than anything else.
◉Spot it
Scenario: the nightly run meets a bad price list

Source: a supplier's price list

Stimulus: contains a row that cannot be parsed

Environment: the nightly run, at 03:10

Response: the row is set aside and reported; the run continues

Measure: the run finishes in good time for the warehouse
Show the answer

Answer The measure has no number. "In good time" cannot fail, so two people can read this scenario and each believe their design passes it. The sign is a measure you could not write a test for. The fix is a figure and a frequency: "the run is finished by 05:30 on 99 nights in 100, and the rejected rows are listed in the 06:00 report".

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Which three characteristics decided this design, and which one did you give up to get them?
  2. For each of the three, what is the scenario, and what number says it passed?
  3. Name one thing this system does today, written down nowhere, that would get someone phoned at home if it stopped.

Still argued: how many characteristics a design should answer to. One side holds that an architect should work through a complete quality model, as ISO/IEC 25010 (2011) provides, and collect scenarios for every attribute that applies, as Bass, Clements and Kazman (1998, with the scenario form from 2003) do. A quality nobody examined, on this view, is a risk nobody saw. The other side, put most plainly by Richards and Ford (2020), holds that every characteristic a design supports complicates it, and that a ranked list of fourteen still tempts a team to build for all fourteen. The architect's job is then to keep the list as short as possible; three is this book's working number. The positions meet in practice: review against the long list so that nothing implicit is missed, and design for the short one.

What Ana learned

  • Separate what the system does from how well it must do it, and take the second list to the people who run it at night.
  • Pick three driving characteristics for each system and say aloud which qualities you are not designing for.
  • Turn each driver into a scenario with a number before anyone draws a box.

…but

With three drivers named, Marcus had a proposal within a week: retire the nightly price table and put a pricing service in its place that works out each price when asked and announces every change as an event. It passes the price-change scenario with four minutes to spare. Everyone in the room liked it, and nobody asked what it gives up.

Chapter 3 · Act INothing Is Free#

The problem

Marcus's proposal fitted on one slide. Retire the nightly price table. Put a pricing service in its place that works out a price when asked and publishes every change as an event. The slide had a column headed Benefits: live prices, the new scenario passed, no nine-million-row recalculation, a design that will scale. He wanted a decision that month, and he had a reason: every week without one, two teams built on the old assumption.

Ingrid was against it and could not say why in a form anyone could act on. "It will break invoicing" is a feeling until someone shows how. Her advice was to wait until more was known.

Ana had seen a benefits column before: Bramble had once split two services on the strength of one, and later merged them back. So she did not vote. She put the three scenarios from the previous chapter on the wall and asked the same question of each: what does this proposal do to it?

The price-change scenario passed. The six o'clock scenario improved. At the third, an invoice anyone can reproduce to the penny, the room went quiet, and then Ingrid could say it. Invoices are run from the same table the order was taken against, and every night's table is kept for seven years. When an auditor asks why account 2217 was charged £43.05 on the third of March, somebody looks it up. Under the proposal there is nothing to look up. The price exists for the length of one request. Marcus's team had a prototype pricing two test accounts that way, and when Ana asked finance to reproduce one of its invoices from the week before, they could not.

The idea

The honest answer to most architecture questions is "it depends", and it is useless unless you say on what. A trade-off is the cathedral ceiling and the heating bill: you may have the ceiling, and you will pay the bill, and the only real mistake is not knowing that the two arrive together. Trade-off analysis is the habit of taking each option to each driving scenario and writing down what it does there, losses beside gains. Marcus's slide was not wrong. It was half a table.

The formal version is the architecture trade-off analysis method, from the Software Engineering Institute. Run in full it takes days and a room of stakeholders, which is more than most decisions deserve. Its vocabulary is worth having for any decision:

  • A utility tree breaks "a good system" into characteristics and then into scenarios, each rated for how much it matters and how hard it is to achieve.
  • A sensitivity point is a decision that one characteristic depends on heavily.
  • A trade-off point is a decision that is a sensitivity point for two characteristics, in opposite directions. These are the decisions worth a meeting.

Quill's tree has one trade-off point, and it is the wall from chapter 1. Fix the price at midnight and every invoice can be reproduced, but nothing changes during the day. Fix it at the moment of asking and it can change at will, but nothing records what it was.

A cheaper way to find such points is risk storming. Put the diagram of the proposal on a wall. Everyone, alone and without talking, sticks a note on each place they think it will go wrong, coloured by how likely and how bad. Then compare. Where the notes pile up there is a risk, and where one person has put a red note that nobody else did there is usually a piece of knowledge the room lacks. At Quill, Ingrid's lone red note was on the arrow from invoicing to the price table.

Having found the cost, Ana still had to decide, and here two more ideas do the work. A two-way door is hanging a door: if it is in the wrong place, you move it. A one-way door is pouring the foundations. Marcus's proposal looked like one decision and was two. Working out a price on request, for quotes, is a two-way door: the table stays, and if the new path misbehaves it is switched off. Retiring the table is a one-way door: seven years of audit answers and an upload format with no price column rest on it. The rule is to decide two-way doors quickly and close to the work, and one-way doors slowly and in the open. Its limit is the case where delay is itself the one-way door, a contract that lapses or a competitor that ships, and then you walk through knowingly and write down what you could not check.

For the one-way door, the question is when. The last responsible moment is ordering the windows when the walls are up: not before, when you would be guessing the sizes, and not after the rain has come in. It is the point after which not deciding removes an option. For the price table, that moment is when invoicing itself is next rebuilt, and not this month. Deferring has a cost too, because people are waiting, so the moment gets a name and a date instead of "later".

The decision Ana took was neither proposal nor refusal. Quotes are worked out on request, the quoted price is stored on the order line, and the nightly table stays as the record invoices are checked against. Marcus's urgency would have been right had the whole proposal been a two-way door, and Ingrid's wish to wait would have been right had nothing been blocked in the meantime. That is not the best architecture. There is no best one. It is the least-worst: the option whose losses, for these three drivers, the company can most easily live with. Its loss is written down too: a price is now worked out in two places, and they must agree.

Remember it as: ask of every proposal what it gives up; if the answer is nothing, you have not found it yet.

◷How we got hereArchitecture reviews in the 1990s were contests of opinion, won by seniority.

Architecture reviews in the 1990s were contests of opinion, won by seniority. Rick Kazman, Mark Klein and Paul Clements at the Software Engineering Institute answered with the architecture trade-off analysis method, published as a report in 2000, which made reviewers state scenarios and find the decisions where qualities pull against each other. Mary and Tom Poppendieck made the last responsible moment a software term in 2003, applying lean thinking to development in reaction to plans that fixed every decision before anything was known. Jeff Bezos gave the doors their names in the shareholder letter published in 2016, complaining that large companies use the heavy process meant for irreversible decisions on reversible ones and become slow. Simon Brown's risk storming (2012) made the review visual and quick, and Richards and Ford (2020) supplied the phrase least-worst. Analysis paralysis is an older name, catalogued with other antipatterns by William Brown and colleagues in 1998.

⚠The traps
  • Best practice without context: the sign is a justification that ends at "it's best practice" with no scenario attached. A practice is best for the drivers it was invented for, which may not be yours.
  • Analysis paralysis: the sign is a third workshop about a choice that could be reversed in a week. The analysis now costs more than being wrong would.
  • The one-way door walked through casually: the sign is "we can always change it later" said of a data format, a published interface or a record being retired. Later arrives with seven years of data in the old shape.
  • The two-way door decided by committee: the sign is a steering group scheduled to choose a library or name a queue. The team waits a month for a decision it could have tried and undone in a day.
  • Benefits listed without costs: the sign is a proposal with a gains column only, and silence when someone asks what it makes harder. The costs exist; they have just not been looked for.
  • Copying a famous company: the sign is a justification that names a firm a thousand times your size. Its architecture answers its drivers, and it employs the people to run it.
◉Spot it

A decision note from Bramble's platform team:

Uploaded order spreadsheets will be kept in the object store instead of the database. Reads are about 40 ms slower, and no customer-facing path reads them. Storage cost falls by two thirds. Files are also kept in the database for 30 days, so we can switch back. The key format for the files was picked in ten minutes; it can be changed later if it turns out wrong.

Show the answer

Answer The key format is a one-way door walked through casually. Everything else here is sound. But within a year millions of files and every program that reads them will depend on that key. The sign is the phrase "can be changed later" attached to a format that data will accumulate in. The fix is to give the key an afternoon and a second reader now, or to store a lookup from upload id to key so that the format stays a two-way door.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What does this proposal make worse, and for which of the three driving scenarios?
  2. Which part of this decision could we undo in a week, and which part could we never undo?
  3. On what date, or at what event, does not deciding start to remove an option?

Still argued: when to decide. Mary and Tom Poppendieck (2003) hold that commitment should be deferred to the last responsible moment, because an early decision is made with the least knowledge the team will ever have. Options kept open are worth more than a tidy plan. Rebecca Wirfs-Brock (2011) replies that designers, herself included, cannot reliably tell when the last moment is until it has passed. The aim should be the most responsible moment, which is often earlier. Marcus's wish to decide that month and Ingrid's wish to wait were these two positions. Both agree the worst outcome is deciding by default, which is what a missed moment amounts to.

What Ana learned

  • Take every proposal to each driving scenario and write what it does there, with the losses beside the gains.
  • Split a proposal into its doors, decide the two-way ones this week, and give each one-way door a date.
  • Choose the least-worst option for the three drivers, and write down the loss you accepted.

…but

The two-way door needs the nightly run and the new request path to produce the same price to the penny, every time. "Then you had better find out where pricing lives," Ingrid said. "It isn't in one place." Last month's change to a single rounding rule had touched thirty-one files.

Chapter 4 · Act IWhat Belongs Together#

The problem

Kofi's team went looking for where pricing lives. It lives in quill-common, a library that also holds date formatting and the code that sends email, and that library is compiled into three programs: order entry, the nightly batch and the reporting tool. The class that prices a line is the same class in all three, by copy.

Finance had asked for one change to it: round each case to the penny, not each order line. The change was eight lines. It was also thirty-one files, because the price passes through every layer of every program on its way to a screen or a table. And it had to go out in all three programs on the same night.

It did not. Order entry was released on the Thursday. The batch was held back by a failing test and went out the following Tuesday. For five nights quotes were rounded one way and the price table the other, and 212 invoices went out a penny or two away from what the customer had been shown. Nothing had crashed. Each program was correct by its own tests.

Marcus's answer was the standard one: a rule should exist in one place, so make pricing a single shared thing that everybody uses. Ingrid pointed at the library. "That is what this was."

The idea

Cohesion is about the inside of one unit: rooms that belong in one building. Pricing rules, discount bands and rounding belong together. Pricing, date formatting and email do not, and a library that holds all three will be changed for three unrelated reasons.

Coupling is about the space between units: buildings that share a wall, a boiler or a drain. It has a direction. Afferent coupling counts who depends on you, and tells you how dangerous you are to change. Efferent coupling counts whom you depend on, and tells you how easily you break. quill-common has an afferent coupling of three programs, so every change to it is three releases.

Connascence says what the other two leave vague. Two things are connascent when a change to one requires a change to the other for the system to stay correct: the lock and every copy of the key. It comes in kinds. Static kinds can be seen by reading the code: two places must agree on a name, a type, the meaning of a value (prices are in pence), the order of arguments, or an algorithm. Dynamic kinds exist only while the system runs: two things must happen in a certain order, within a certain time, with values that match, or on the very same object. And it has three properties:

  • Strength: how hard the dependence is to see and to change. A shared name is weak; a shared algorithm is stronger; anything dynamic is stronger still.
  • Locality: how far apart the two things are. Inside one class, even strong connascence is harmless. Across teams or across a network it is not.
  • Degree: how many things are bound. Two is manageable. Thirty-one files in three programs is not.

Quill's five bad nights were connascence of algorithm, at a distance, with a degree of three: three programs that had to round identically and could be released on different days.

Cohesion Coupling Connascence
Asks Do the things inside belong together? How much does this unit depend on others? Exactly what must change together?
Looks Within one unit Between units: afferent in, efferent out Between any two elements
At Quill The library holds pricing, dates and email: low Three programs depend on it All three must round the same way
You want High Low, or at least known Weak, or else close together

The rule that follows is to keep strong connascence close and let only the weak kind travel. Its limit is that weakening always costs something, usually a layer of indirection, and inside one small unit that cost buys nothing.

Two more words turn this into something an architect can arrange. A component is a wing with its own entrance: a named part of the system with one job and a stated way in, whether it is built as a package, a module or a service. How the components are cut is the first structural decision. Technical partitioning cuts by kind of code: presentation, business logic, persistence. Domain partitioning cuts by what the business does: pricing, ordering, invoicing. Quill is partitioned technically, which is why one pricing rule crossed thirty-one files. Technical partitioning is the right cut when the changes you expect are technical ones, such as replacing the database. Most changes are not. How to find the domain's own borders is the Atlas's subject, chapter 6.

The last word is the one the rest of this book leans on. An architecture quantum is what must be built, opened and closed together: the smallest part of a system that can be deployed on its own, counting everything it cannot run without, its database included. Quill has three programs and one quantum, because all three share a database and a library. That is why the release in two halves failed, and why characteristics are chosen per quantum. Inside one quantum, everything gets the same availability, the same release day and the same bad night.

So the repair was modest. Pricing became one component with one entrance and one owning team. The reporting tool stopped pricing anything and now reads stored prices, which takes the degree from three to two. And the release process refuses to ship order entry without the batch, which admits in the open what was always true: they are one quantum. Marcus was right that the rule needed one home. Ingrid was right that a library copied into three programs is not one, and his argument fails only where the single thing is shared by copying.

Remember it as: keep together what changes together, and make sure that what is far apart can change alone.

◷How we got hereDavid Parnas argued in 1972 that a system should be divided by the decisions most likely to change, not by…

David Parnas argued in 1972 that a system should be divided by the decisions most likely to change, not by the steps of its processing. Wayne Stevens, Glenford Myers and Larry Constantine supplied the two measuring words, coupling and cohesion, in "Structured Design" (1974), reacting to programs in which any change rippled everywhere. Meilir Page-Jones found those words too blunt for object-oriented code and in 1992 proposed connascence, which names the kind of agreement that binds two things; his 1995 book added the dynamic forms, and later writers, notably Jim Weirich, added strength, locality and degree. Distributed systems made distance matter again, and Vlad Khononov's Balancing Coupling in Software Design (2024) restates the idea as strength, distance and volatility. Ford, Parsons and Kua named the architectural quantum in 2017. Richards and Ford (2020) named the entity trap, below.

⚠The traps
  • The shared library as hidden coupling: the sign is a common or utils library that holds a business rule and is compiled into several programs. They must be released together or they disagree, and nothing in the build says so.
  • The entity trap: the sign is components named after tables, such as Customer Manager, Order Manager and Product Manager, each offering create, read, update and delete. That is the database with a class in front of it; behaviour such as pricing an order has no home and ends up in every caller.
  • Dynamic connascence across a network: the sign is two services that only work when called in a certain order or within a certain time, with a wiki page as the only record. It is the strongest kind of dependence at the greatest distance, and it fails intermittently.
  • Technical partitioning for domain change: the sign is that every business change touches every layer and needs the screen team, the services team and the database team in one meeting. The cut runs across the direction of change.
◉Spot it
Show the answer

Answer The components are the tables with "Manager" added: the entity trap. The sign is that each component's name is a noun from the schema and its interface is four data operations. Nothing here prices an order or checks a credit limit, so that behaviour will be written in the screens, three times. The fix is to cut by what the business does, for example Pricing, Ordering and Account Credit, and let each own the tables it needs.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. If this rule changes, how many separately released things must change with it, and can they go out on different days?
  2. Name the last three business changes: how many components did each one touch?
  3. What must be deployed together for this feature to work, counting its database?

Still argued: share a rule or duplicate it. Andrew Hunt and David Thomas (1999) hold that every piece of knowledge should have one authoritative representation, because two copies of a rule will drift and a business with two pricing rules has two prices. This was Marcus's argument for a single shared pricing component. Sandi Metz (2016) holds that duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction, because shared code binds every user to one shape and one release. The cost of that binding is paid on every later change. The two are not strict opposites, since the first is about knowledge and the second about code that merely looks alike, and practice has settled part of this: inside one component, do not repeat yourself. Across separately released programs it is still a judgement, between the drift of two copies and the lock of one.

What Ana learned

  • When something breaks far from the change, name the connascence: what had to change together, how strongly, how far apart and how many.
  • Cut components by what the business changes, and keep the technical layers inside them.
  • Draw the quantum before promising that anything is independent, because whatever shares a database or a library ships together.

…but

Marcus's interim report arrived the same week. It called Quill "a legacy layered monolith" and named the layering as the root cause. Ingrid read it standing up. "It is one building with floors. It has taken three hundred orders an hour for fifteen years without anyone thinking about it. Which part of that is wrong?"

Chapter 5 · Act IIThe Terrace#

The problem

Marcus's report said that layers group code by what it is and not by what changes together, so that every business change is smeared across the whole program, and it recommended replacing the layered design. Ingrid's reply was that layers are simple, cheap, understood by every developer Quill has ever hired, and have carried order entry for fifteen years. Each was repeating a position with a long history, and Ana had no way to choose between them except by liking one of them more.

So Kofi counted. He took the last forty changes made to order entry. Thirty-three had touched one screen and the code directly beneath it, and had been done by one developer in under two days. Seven had been pricing changes, and those were the thirty-one-file kind. Then he traced two hundred kinds of request through the program. Forty-six of them passed through the middle layer without the middle layer doing anything to them at all.

He also found something nobody had decided. The reporting tool does not go through the business layer. In 2014 someone made one report faster by reading the tables directly, and the trick was copied into every report since. Last year a discount rule was added to the business layer, the reports never saw it, and an account manager walked into a contract renewal with a spend figure £1,900 lower than the customer's own invoices.

The idea

The layered style is the terrace: every house has the same floors in the same order. This chapter looks at it as the shape of a whole system. What the inside of one deployable should look like, and the styles that turn the layers inside out, belong to the Atlas, chapter 9.

The parts. Horizontal layers, each with one technical job: presentation, business, persistence, and the database underneath. Every feature the system has is cut across all of them. Quill's five capabilities do not appear as parts at all; each is a strip running down through every floor.

How they talk. A request enters at the top and is passed down by ordinary calls inside one process; the answer comes back up the same way. A layer is closed when a request must go through it and may not skip to the one below. Layers are closed by default, because closure is what the style sells: a change to how data is stored can reach the business layer and no further. An open layer is one that requests are allowed to bypass. Opening one is legitimate when the layer adds nothing for a whole class of requests, read-only reports being the usual case, and it has a price: everything above now depends on two layers instead of one, so a change below travels further. An open layer that was decided and written down is a design. One that was discovered, like Quill's reports, is a leak.

Where the data lives. In one database, reached only through the persistence layer. Nothing in the style says which tables belong to which capability, so in time every query joins whatever is convenient.

Strong and weak. The style is strong on simplicity and on cost: one program, one build, one thing to run, and no developer needs it explained. Testability is fair, since a layer can be tested against a stand-in for the one below. It is weak on deployability, because every change ships the whole building; on elasticity and fault tolerance, because the building scales and fails as one; and on evolvability whenever the change is to the business and not to the technology.

The cost of leaving. Low if the layers have stayed closed: the same code can be re-cut by domain, one capability at a time. High if they have leaked, because the first job is discovering what depends on what.

When a request passes through a layer that does nothing but hand it on, that is a sinkhole: a floor you only walk through to reach the stairs. Some are normal. The working rule is about proportion: if roughly a fifth of requests are sinkholes, the layers are earning their keep on the rest; if most are, the system is paying for isolation it does not use. Order entry's forty-six in two hundred is acceptable. The reporting tool's figure would be nearly all of them, which is why somebody opened that layer by accident. The repair is to open it on purpose, for reports only, and to have reports read stored prices and never recompute one.

The alternative Marcus was reaching for has a name, the modular monolith: one building with fire walls between the wings.

Layered Modular monolith
Cut by Technical role Business capability; each module keeps its own layers inside
A pricing change touches Every layer One module
Borders enforced Between layers, by convention Between modules, by the build
Data One schema; any query may join any table One database, a schema per module
Deploy unit One One

The Atlas, chapters 9 and 21, covers how to build one and when it is the default.

So when is layered the right answer? When the team is small, the work is mostly data in and data out, changes stay within one screen and the code beneath it, and the driving characteristics are simplicity and cost. Thirty-three of order entry's last forty changes were exactly that. Order entry stays a terrace, and Ingrid was right about it. Marcus was right about the other seven: pricing changes cut across the floors, which is why pricing became a component with its own entrance in the last chapter. His premise, that business changes cross every layer, fails here only because most of order entry's changes are not that kind. In a system where most are, with several teams, it holds.

Remember it as: every house has the same floors in the same order: cheap to build, and a change to the business climbs every floor.

◷How we got hereEdsger Dijkstra described the THE operating system in 1968 as a stack of layers, each built only on the one…

Edsger Dijkstra described the THE operating system in 1968 as a stack of layers, each built only on the one beneath, so that each could be reasoned about and tested before the next was added. That was a reaction to systems too tangled to verify. Business software adopted the idea in the 1990s as three tiers, reacting to client programs that kept their rules in the screens, and Frank Buschmann and his co-authors wrote it up as the Layers pattern in 1996. By then it was simply how applications were built, which is how most layered systems come to exist without anyone choosing the style. Mark Richards (2015) wrote up its commonest failure as the sinkhole, with the one-fifth rule of thumb, while still recommending the style as a sound general-purpose start.

⚠The traps
  • The sinkhole: the sign is a chain of methods with the same name in each layer, each calling the next and adding nothing. If most requests look like that, the layers are ceremony.
  • The accidentally open layer: the sign is a query in a screen or a report that reads tables directly, with no record of anyone deciding it. A rule added to the skipped layer silently fails to apply there.
  • Lasagne: the sign is seven or eight thin layers, with facades, managers and mappers between the usual three, so that adding one field edits a file in each. Isolation has been bought several times over and is paid for on every change.
  • Layered by default: the sign is that nobody can say why the system is layered except that the project template was. It is often fine; the trap is not noticing when the changes stop being the kind that layers make cheap.
◉Spot it

A team's own drawing of its module. No document of theirs says that a layer may be skipped.

Show the answer

Answer The statement screens call the persistence layer directly, so the business layer is open for them and nothing says that anyone chose this. The sign is one arrow that skips a floor. A statement shows what an account owes, which depends on the pricing and credit rules it has bypassed, so it will disagree with the invoices the first time a rule changes. The fix is to route statements through the business layer, or to open the layer deliberately for figures that are stored and never recomputed, and record that.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Of the last twenty changes, how many touched more than one layer, and how many needed more than one team?
  2. Which layers are open, and where is the decision to open each one recorded?
  3. What share of requests pass through a layer that does nothing to them?

Still argued: whether layered should still be anyone's default. Mark Richards (2015) holds that it is a sound general-purpose style and a reasonable place to start when the right style is not yet clear. It is cheap, familiar and easy to staff. Jimmy Bogard (2018) holds that layers join code that does not change together and separate code that does. Organising by feature from the first day avoids paying to re-cut it later. The two disagree about what most changes look like, and that can be measured in any existing system by doing what Kofi did. For a new system there is nothing to count, and the argument stays open.

What Ana learned

  • Count before condemning a style: how many changes crossed its boundaries, and how many requests passed through a part that did nothing.
  • Keep layers closed by default, and when one is opened, write down which, for what, and what it costs in isolation.
  • Leave a simple system in a simple style when its drivers are simplicity and cost.

…but

The report had called the nightly batch layered as well. It is not layers. It is six thousand lines that do one thing after another, and that night it stopped at 03:10 on a malformed row in one supplier's price list. There was no way to restart it from the middle. It began again from the top and finished at 07:25.

Chapter 6 · Act IIThe Assembly Line#

The problem

The nightly run is one procedure of six thousand lines. It starts at one in the morning, when the last supplier's file is due, and takes about four hours. It works through thirty-eight suppliers in turn, importing each list and recalculating the prices that depend on it, then prices the day's uploaded orders, produces the invoices and sends the couriers their manifests, sharing a set of working tables and several running totals held in memory.

At 03:10 it met a price written 4,85 by a new supplier in Rotterdam and stopped. Twenty-two suppliers had already been imported. Nobody could restart it from the twenty-third, because nobody could say which working tables were half written and which totals had been lost with the process. Running it again from that point risked applying twenty-two price lists twice. So it ran again from the top and finished at 07:25. The warehouse stood for eighty-five minutes. It was the third overrun of the quarter, and the second driving characteristic from chapter 2, finished by six, had now been failed in public.

Ingrid explained the design without defending it. When she joined, the whole run took forty minutes, and starting again cost nothing anyone noticed. Marcus proposed removing the batch altogether: treat every price change as an event in a stream, and there is no window to miss. Ingrid's answer was that the suppliers send one file a day whatever Quill builds, and that recomputing from those files each night is the one design she knows how to prove correct.

The idea

Work that flows in one direction, through steps that each do one thing, has its own style. The pipeline style, also called pipes and filters, is the assembly line: each station does one thing and passes it on.

The parts. Filters and pipes. A filter is a station; a pipe is the conveyor between two stations. Filters come in four kinds. A producer starts the line: it reads a supplier's file. A transformer takes what arrives, changes it and passes it on: convert the cost to pounds, apply the account's contract terms. A tester checks each item and either passes it on or diverts it: a row that cannot be parsed goes to a rejects pile. A consumer ends the line: it writes the price table or sends a manifest.

How they talk. One way only. A filter reads from the pipe behind it and writes to the pipe in front. It does not know which station comes next, never calls another filter, and never reaches back for something an earlier one had. The pipe carries one agreed format. In code the whole contract is a single method:

public record PriceListRow(String supplier, String sku, Money cost,
                           LocalDate validFrom) {}

public interface PriceListFilter {
    Stream<PriceListRow> apply(Stream<PriceListRow> rows);
}

And one transformer, which keeps nothing between one row and the next:

public final class ToSterling implements PriceListFilter {
    private final Map<Currency, BigDecimal> ratesAtMidnight;

    public ToSterling(Map<Currency, BigDecimal> ratesAtMidnight) {
        this.ratesAtMidnight = Map.copyOf(ratesAtMidnight);
    }

    @Override
    public Stream<PriceListRow> apply(Stream<PriceListRow> rows) {
        return rows.map(r -> new PriceListRow(
            r.supplier(), r.sku(), toSterling(r.cost()), r.validFrom()));
    }

    private Money toSterling(Money cost) {
        var rate = ratesAtMidnight.get(cost.currency());
        long pence = rate.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(cost.minorUnits()))
            .setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).longValueExact();
        return new Money(pence, Currency.getInstance("GBP"));
    }
}

Money is the record the Atlas defines in its chapter 10, an amount in minor units and a currency. The line itself is a list of such filters applied in order.

Where the data lives. In the pipes. Between stations the work in progress sits in the pipe, and for a nightly run the pipe should be something that survives a crash: a file or a staging table named for the run and the station. The filters themselves own nothing.

Strong and weak. Strong on simplicity, testability and evolvability: a station is tested with a file in and a file out, and a new one is slotted in without touching the others. It is cheap to run. Fault tolerance is fair, and only if the re-run is designed. It is weak on deployability and elasticity when the line is one deployable, and it cannot hold a conversation. There is no way back up the line, so anything that must answer a waiting customer, such as taking an order at a screen, does not belong on it.

The cost of leaving. Low. Filters are small and know nothing of each other, so they can be moved into separate jobs or rented functions one at a time. The pipe format is the part worth keeping.

Re-running is where the style pays for itself, and it has to be built in. Each station writes its whole output to a durable pipe, or none of it. Each station can be run twice on the same input and leave the same result, replacing what it wrote before instead of adding to it. The run records which stations have finished, so a restart begins at the first that has not. And bad input is diverted by a tester, never thrown, so that one supplier's comma does not stop the other thirty-seven. The rule is that every station must be safe to repeat. Its limit is a consumer that acts on the outside world: a manifest sent to a courier twice is two collections. That station needs a record of what it has sent, or a reference the other side uses to discard repeats, and keeping that record is the cost.

A pipeline is not workflow orchestration. On a line, data moves one way through stations of one shape, and the only choice is pass or divert. In a workflow a coordinator runs steps of different kinds, waits for people or other systems, branches, and undoes earlier steps when a later one fails. The moment a design says "if station four fails, reverse station two", it has stopped being a pipeline and become the saga of the Atlas, chapter 16. A scheduler that starts the stations in order does not change the style.

Quill's run was rebuilt as fourteen stations. The batch stayed a batch, and Ingrid was right about that: the input arrives once a day, and the nightly price table is what makes an invoice reproducible. Marcus's stream is the better design where data arrives all day and answers are wanted all day, which the system design book takes up in chapter 12. The next malformed row went to the rejects pile, and that night's run finished at 04:50 as usual.

Remember it as: each station does one thing, keeps nothing and passes it on, so any station can be tested alone and run again.

◷How we got hereDoug McIlroy wrote a memorandum at Bell Labs in 1964 wishing for a way of connecting programs "like garden…

Doug McIlroy wrote a memorandum at Bell Labs in 1964 wishing for a way of connecting programs "like garden hose", screwing in another segment when data needed massaging another way. Ken Thompson built it into Unix in 1973 as the pipe, and small programs that each did one thing became the Unix habit, in reaction to large programs that could not be recombined. David Garlan and Mary Shaw's "An Introduction to Software Architecture" (1993) listed pipes and filters among the first catalogued architectural styles, and Buschmann and his co-authors wrote it up, with its consequences, as a pattern in 1996.

⚠The traps
  • Filters that share state: the sign is a static field, a shared working table or a running total that two stations both touch. No station can then be repeated or reordered on its own, which is exactly why Quill's run could not restart.
  • The filter that does everything: the sign is one station called "process" with six jobs and a thousand lines. It cannot be tested with a small file, and when it fails all six jobs start again.
  • The pipeline with no re-run story: the sign is that nobody can say, for a failure at station seven at 03:10, which stations run again and what would be written twice. The answer is discovered at 03:10.
◉Spot it
public final class DropDuplicates implements PriceListFilter {
    private static final Set<PriceListRow> seen = new HashSet<>();

    @Override
    public Stream<PriceListRow> apply(Stream<PriceListRow> rows) {
        return rows.filter(seen::add);
    }
}
Show the answer

Answer The set of rows already seen is static, so it outlives the call and is shared by every use of the filter in the process. Run the station a second time on the same file and every row is a duplicate: the output is empty. The sign is a mutable static field in a filter. The fix is to create the set inside apply, so that each run starts clean and the station can be repeated.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. If station seven fails at 03:10, which stations run again, and what is written twice?
  2. Can each station be tested with a file in and a file out, and nothing else running?
  3. Where does a bad row go, and who reads that place in the morning?

Still argued: batch or stream. Nathan Marz (2011) holds that the dependable design keeps the raw input unchanged and recomputes results from it in batch, because a recomputation corrects any earlier mistake, with a separate fast path only for what cannot wait. This was Ingrid's case for the nightly run. Jay Kreps (2014) holds that keeping a batch path and a fast path means writing every rule twice, and that a single stream processor, replaying its input when the logic changes, does both jobs with one body of code. This was Marcus's. Neither has displaced the other. The choice follows how the input arrives and how soon the answer is needed.

What Ana learned

  • Give work that flows one way an assembly line, and give every station one job and no memory.
  • Design the re-run before the run: durable pipes, stations that can be repeated, and a record of which have finished.
  • Divert bad input to a place someone reads, so that one row never stops the line.

…but

The last station is courier booking, and it is one class with a branch for each courier: Quill's three, and Bramble's two since the merger. Lena has announced a partner programme, twenty partners within the year. Adding the sixth courier last week changed a helper that formats labels, and for a morning the second courier's depot refused every parcel Quill sent.

Chapter 7 · Act IIThe Hall and Its Stalls#

The problem

Courier booking is one class with a branch for each courier. There are six branches now, and they share helpers: one for labels, one for postcodes, one for weights. The sixth courier, a pallet carrier taken on for Bramble's bulky orders, needed the label helper to print a longer reference. The change was tested against the new courier. The next morning the second courier's depot refused 340 parcels, because its scanners could not read the longer label.

Every courier added is a change to the code all the others run through, a retest of all of them, and a seat on the fortnightly release. Lena's partner programme promises twenty integrations within the year: more couriers, a tax calculator for sales to Ireland and the Netherlands, suppliers who want to send price lists in their own formats, and eventually partners who write their own.

Marcus proposed a service for each integration: separately deployed, with a published interface that cannot be bypassed, and a clear owner. Ingrid looked at what each one does. They all do the same job, in about two hundred lines, with a different courier at the far end. Twenty more things to deploy and watch, for twenty small variations of one thing, seemed to her the wrong size of answer.

The idea

When one job has many variations, and the variations come and go, the style that fits is the microkernel style, also called the plug-in architecture. It is the market hall and its stalls: the hall provides the roof and the rules, and the stalls come and go.

The parts. A core system and plug-ins. The core holds only what is always true: take a parcel that is ready, find a courier that can carry it, ask for a booking, record the result. A plug-in holds one variation: everything about one courier and nothing about any other. Two smaller parts make it work. The contract says what every plug-in must offer and what it is given. The registry is how the core finds out which plug-ins exist and what each can do.

How they talk. The core calls a plug-in through the contract, usually as an ordinary call inside one process. A plug-in never calls another plug-in, and it knows the core only by what the contract passes in.

public interface CourierPlugin {
    String id();
    int contractVersion();
    boolean canCarry(Parcel parcel);
    Booking book(Parcel parcel);
}

public record Parcel(OrderId orderId, int grams, String postcode,
                     Money declaredValue) {}
public record Booking(String courierId, String trackingNumber, Money charge) {}

The registry is a lookup, and it is also where a plug-in built for the wrong contract is turned away:

public final class PluginRegistry {
    private static final int SUPPORTED = 2;
    private final Map<String, CourierPlugin> plugins = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    public void register(CourierPlugin plugin) {
        if (plugin.contractVersion() != SUPPORTED)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(plugin.id()
                + " was built for contract " + plugin.contractVersion());
        plugins.put(plugin.id(), plugin);
    }

    public Optional<CourierPlugin> firstAbleToCarry(Parcel parcel) {
        return plugins.values().stream()
            .filter(p -> p.canCarry(parcel)).findFirst();
    }
}

One stall, complete:

public final class NorthlinePlugin implements CourierPlugin {
    private final NorthlineClient client;

    public NorthlinePlugin(NorthlineClient client) { this.client = client; }

    @Override public String id() { return "northline"; }
    @Override public int contractVersion() { return 2; }

    @Override public boolean canCarry(Parcel parcel) {
        return parcel.grams() <= 30_000;
    }

    @Override public Booking book(Parcel parcel) {
        var label = client.createLabel(parcel.postcode(), parcel.grams());
        return new Booking(id(), label.tracking(), label.charge());
    }
}

Where the data lives. With the core. A plug-in is handed what it needs in the call and hands back a result. It has no connection to the core's tables. Anything of its own, such as a courier's service codes, it keeps itself.

Strong and weak. Strong on evolvability, testability and simplicity: a courier is added without touching the core or any other courier, and is tested alone against the contract. Cost is low. Deployability is fair: better than a plain monolith if stalls can be added without redeploying the hall, no better if they cannot. It is weak on elasticity and fault tolerance, because everything is under one roof.

The cost of leaving. Low. The contract is already a boundary, so a plug-in can be moved into its own process behind the same contract, one at a time. The exception is a core that has grown fat, which must be thinned first.

Two things about the contract decide whether the hall survives its tenth stall. The first is versioning. The contract will change; sales to Ireland need a customs declaration no courier call carries today. So the contract has a version number, each plug-in declares the version it was built for, and the registry refuses a mismatch at start-up instead of failing on a parcel at two in the morning. While one team writes every plug-in and they all ship in one release, the number is ceremony, and it is reasonable to leave it out; the cost is that it must be added on the day the first outsider writes a stall, and by then there are twenty to update.

The second is isolation. A stall that catches fire is inside the hall. Every call to a plug-in gets a time limit, and a failure is caught at the contract and recorded against that courier alone. If plug-ins are written by people you do not employ, they run in a separate process behind the same contract, which costs a network hop and something more to operate.

The style is easily confused with the one whose name it nearly shares:

Microkernel Microservices
The parts A core, and plug-ins that all do the same kind of job Services that each do a different job
Who is in charge The core calls the plug-ins Nobody; services deal with each other as equals
Runs as Usually one process Many processes
Data With the core Each service owns its own
A part failing Can take the hall down unless isolated Is contained, if the others can cope without it
Suits Many variations of one thing Many different things with different owners

Courier booking became a hall. The supplier formats did too, as the first station of chapter 6's line, which makes that station a small hall on an assembly line; styles combine, and chapter 13 returns to that. Ingrid's size of answer was the right one while one team writes every stall. Marcus's premise, that each integration needs its own deployment and owner, fails for six couriers maintained by four people. It will hold for the stalls that partners write themselves, and the contract is what will let those move out.

Remember it as: the hall provides the roof and the rules; a stall can arrive, change or leave without the hall or its neighbours noticing.

◷How we got hereThe word comes from operating systems.

The word comes from operating systems. Research projects of the 1980s, the best known being Mach at Carnegie Mellon, begun in 1985, reacted to kernels that had grown to contain everything by working towards a minimal kernel with file systems and drivers moved outside it. Frank Buschmann and his co-authors generalised the idea to applications as the Microkernel pattern in 1996, for products that had to be adapted to many customers without editing the product each time. The style became familiar through tools: Erich Gamma and Kent Beck's Contributing to Eclipse (2003) describes a development environment in which everything, including its own features, is a plug-in. James Lewis and Martin Fowler's microservices article (2014) made the opposing case that a component should be a separately deployed service.

⚠The traps
  • Plug-ins that depend on each other: the sign is a plug-in that imports another, or only works if another is loaded first. Stalls can no longer be added or removed one at a time, and the hall has a second structure nobody drew.
  • The fat core: the sign is a plug-in's name in the core, as in if (courier.id().equals("northline")). Every new stall then needs a change to the hall, which is what the style was chosen to avoid.
  • The unversioned contract: the sign is a contract changed in place with every plug-in rebuilt the same night. It works until one plug-in belongs to someone else, and then it fails in production.
  • A plug-in with access to the core's database: the sign is a connection or a repository handed to a plug-in "for convenience". The core's tables are now part of the contract, and the core can never again change them freely.
◉Spot it
Show the answer

Answer The pallet carrier plug-in calls the address check plug-in directly. The sign is an arrow between two stalls. The pallet carrier now fails if the address check is removed, replaced or simply loaded later, and the registry knows nothing about that dependence. The fix is for the core to check the address, through the address contract, before it asks any courier, and to pass the checked address in the parcel.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Can a plug-in be added, changed or removed without editing the core or any other plug-in: yes or no?
  2. Which contract version does each installed plug-in declare, and what does the core do with one it does not support?
  3. If one plug-in hangs for sixty seconds, does the core go on serving the others: yes or no?

Still argued: a plug-in in the same process, or a service per integration. Lewis and Fowler (2014) hold that a component should be a separately deployed service, because a boundary inside one process is kept only by discipline and erodes. A service's published interface cannot be reached around. Gamma and Beck (2003) describe a platform in which everything is a plug-in, loaded into one process by a small kernel and kept orderly by explicit contracts between plug-ins. It has none of the cost of running a process for each. Neither claim has been refuted. What decides between them in practice is who writes the plug-ins and whether they must be released on different days.

What Ana learned

  • When one job has many variations, put the job in a small core and each variation in a plug-in behind one contract.
  • Keep the core ignorant: no plug-in's name appears in it, and no plug-in sees its database.
  • Version the contract before anyone outside the team writes a plug-in, and give every call to a plug-in a time limit.

…but

The hall took its seventh courier in a day. It is still inside one release. Three teams now work on Quill, order entry, pricing and finance, and every change any of them makes leaves on the same fortnightly train. A pricing fix has just waited nine days behind an invoicing change that failed its tests twice. One building has one front door.

Chapter 8 · Act IIIA Handful of Big Buildings#

The problem

Three teams work on Quill now: order entry, pricing and finance. All of their changes leave on one release every other Thursday, and a release goes only if every team's tests pass.

A fault in the volume-break calculation was over-discounting one large account, and the pricing team had the fix ready on a Monday. It sat for nine days behind an invoicing change that failed its tests twice. For nine days the account went on being over-discounted, and Quill gave away £6,400. Nobody had done anything wrong. The fix was simply in the same building as somebody else's unfinished work.

Marcus's proposal was to end the shared release for good: about thirty services, each with its own database and its own pipeline, none able to block another. Ingrid agreed about the release and not about the rest. The database has four hundred tables and fifteen years of queries that join across them. Month-end reconciliation is one query over orders, invoices, payments and credit notes. Giving each of thirty services its own data, she said, is two years' work, and she could not promise the month would still close at the end of it.

Ana asked which characteristic was actually failing. It was not scale and not resilience. It was that three teams could not ship separately.

The idea

There is a style for exactly that, and it is the least dramatic way to become a distributed system. The service-based style is a campus of a few large buildings sharing one records office.

The parts. A small number of coarse-grained domain services, usually between four and twelve. Each is a whole area of the business, is deployed on its own, and is an ordinary layered or modular program inside. A user interface sits in front of them, and one database sits behind.

How they talk. The user interface calls the services. The services call each other as little as possible, directly when they must, and there is nothing in the middle to route or translate. Much of what would be a call between services in other styles is here simply a read from the database.

Where the data lives. In one shared database, logically partitioned: the tables are grouped into a schema for each service, and each schema has exactly one service that writes to it. Other services may read it, by agreement. That rule is the whole difference between this style and the shared database the Atlas warns against in chapter 8, where nobody owns the tables. It has no exception worth having. Reading is another matter: reading another service's schema is allowed because it keeps reports and reconciliations simple, and every such read is a column its owner can no longer rename freely. So the reads are listed, and the list is kept short.

Strong and weak. Strong on deployability: each team ships on its own day. Simplicity and cost are fair, and the best of any distributed style, since there are few things to run and the data has not moved. Testability and evolvability are good, because each service is one area of the business. Fault tolerance and elasticity are only fair: a service can fail or be scaled alone, but every one of them stands on the same database.

The cost of leaving. Low in either direction. Each service with its schema is already cut along a business line, so it can be divided further, or take its tables away with it, when a reason arrives. The services can also be folded back into one program without touching the data.

The style is easiest to understand beside its two relatives. Service-oriented architecture is a campus where every errand goes through the central switchboard, and the switchboard was the enterprise service bus.

Service-oriented architecture Service-based Microservices
Service size Mixed; many small services meant for reuse across the company A whole business area; four to twelve of them One capability; tens or hundreds
Data ownership Shared company databases behind the services One database, one schema and one writer per service A database per service
Coordination A central bus that routes, translates and runs the process The screens, and a few direct calls No centre: calls and events between equals
Deploy unit The service, though most changes also touch the bus The service The service
Reacting to Departmental systems that could not talk to each other One release shared by several teams The bus, and the shared database
