Service-oriented architecture is history now. Its aim was reuse: write "get customer" once and have every system call it through the bus. In practice the bus collected routing rules, then data conversions, then business rules, until every change in the company waited for the team that ran it. Microservices were the reaction: no centre, and nothing shared. The service-based style sits between the two on purpose. It takes separate deployment from microservices and declines to pay for separate data until a characteristic demands it.

Quill's back office became four services over five weeks. The work was not moving data. It was declaring an owner for each table and removing the twenty-three places where one team's code wrote to another's. Dispatch now books the courier as each order is placed, so that the customer can be told a delivery day, and the nightly line sends only the manifest. The pricing team now ships three times a week. Ingrid was right about the data. Marcus was right that the shared release had to end, and his premise, that separate deployment needs separate databases, fails only because deployment was the one thing failing. Where services must scale or fail separately, or one team's schema changes weekly, it holds.

Remember it as: a few big buildings, each with its own door, and its own shelves in one shared records office.

◷How we got hereThomas Erl's Service-Oriented Architecture (2005) is the fullest statement of the idea that a company's…

Thomas Erl's Service-Oriented Architecture (2005) is the fullest statement of the idea that a company's systems should be rebuilt as shared, reusable services joined by a bus, a reaction to departments whose systems could not exchange a customer record. Within a few years the bus had become the place where every project queued. The microservices writers of 2014 reacted in turn with separately owned services and no intelligent middle, which the Atlas covers in its chapter 2. Neal Ford and Mark Richards gave the middle position its name, service-based architecture, in a video course in 2015 and a full chapter in 2020: most teams that say they want microservices want separate deployment, and can have it without first dividing fifteen years of data.

⚠The traps
  • The shared schema that ripples: the sign is a column rename that needs four services deployed on the same night, or a table nobody can name the owner of. The shared release has come back, and this time it is run from the database.
  • The service bus returns: the sign is a "gateway" or "integration layer" between the screens and the services that has begun to make decisions of its own. It is the switchboard again, and every change now needs its team.
  • Service creep: the sign is a service count that goes from five to twenty in a year, each split sensible on its own, all still on one database. That is the running cost of microservices without their independence.
◉Spot it
Show the answer

Answer The ordering schema has two writers: Invoicing sets a flag on orders directly. The sign is two "writes" arrows arriving at one schema. Ordering can no longer change how it stores an order's state without Invoicing deploying too, and when the flag is wrong nobody knows which service set it. The fix is one writer: Invoicing asks Ordering to mark the order, or keeps "invoiced" in its own schema, where it already knows it.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. For each table, which one service writes to it?
  2. When did a schema change last force more than one service to deploy, and how many did it force?
  3. How many services were there a year ago, how many are there now, and does each new one have a recorded reason?

Still argued: whether services may share a database at all. Sam Newman (2015) holds that integration through a shared database is to be avoided at nearly all costs, because every service that can see a table depends on its shape, and that a service which does not own its data is not independently deployable in any sense that matters. This was Marcus's position. Richards and Ford (2020) hold that dividing the data is the most expensive part of distribution, that a single database with one writer per schema keeps transactions and reporting simple, and that the price of separate data should be paid only when a characteristic requires it. This was Ingrid's. The disagreement is about the default. Both sides accept the other's design when the drivers call for it.

What Ana learned

  • Name the characteristic that is failing before deciding how far to split; when it is three teams unable to ship separately, a few big services are enough.
  • Give every table one writing service, and keep a short list of who else reads it.
  • Split the code first, and the data only when a characteristic demands it.

…but

Each team now ships on its own day. But placing an order asks Pricing for a price, then Dispatch for a courier booking, one after the other, while the customer waits. Last Thursday one courier's system was down for forty minutes, and for forty minutes Quill could not take an order.

Chapter 9 · Act IIIThe Noticeboard#

The problem

Placing an order at Quill is now a chain. Ordering asks Pricing for a price, then asks Dispatch to book a courier, and Dispatch asks the courier's own system. The customer waits for all of it.

On Thursday one courier's system was down for forty minutes. Dispatch's calls to it timed out, Ordering's calls to Dispatch timed out behind them, and for forty minutes nobody could place an order. About 190 were lost or phoned in. The courier would not have collected anything until four that afternoon in any case.

There was a second, slower problem. Bramble's marketplace team wanted to know whenever a trade order was placed, to award loyalty points. Finance wanted to know, to track credit exposure. Each asked the Ordering team to add a call to their system. Ordering was acquiring a list of everyone who cared about orders, and every addition was another thing that could stop an order being taken.

Marcus's answer was his target architecture in one sentence: nothing calls anything; every service announces what it has done, and every other service listens. Ingrid's objection was two questions. When a customer is typing an order and needs a price, who are they supposed to wait for? And once nothing calls anything, who can say what happens after an order is placed?

The idea

The event-driven style is the town noticeboard: post a notice, and whoever cares acts on it. An event is a statement that something has happened, order placed, written by the one service that knows, without knowledge of who will read it.

The parts. Event processors, which are services that react to events and post their own; the events; and the channels that carry them, held by a message broker. The event that starts a flow is the initiating event. The ones posted along the way, courier booked, invoice opened, are processing events.

How they talk. Asynchronously. The poster does not wait. There are two ways to arrange who reacts, and they are different enough to count as two styles. In the broker topology, notices are passed hand to hand: each processor reacts to an event and posts another, and the flow is whatever chain of reactions results. In the mediator topology, a clerk reads each notice and assigns the errands: the initiating event goes to one component that knows the steps, tells each processor what to do, and keeps track.

Broker Mediator
Who knows the whole flow Nobody; it emerges The mediator
Adding a reaction Subscribe; nothing else changes Change the mediator
When a step fails Each processor copes alone The mediator retries, reroutes or undoes
Processors depend on The events The mediator's instructions
Suits Simple flows with many independent reactions Flows with a fixed sequence, conditions and steps to undo

The Atlas meets the same choice for sagas in chapter 16, under the names choreography and orchestration. Quill's order flow is a fan of independent reactions, so it uses a broker. Returns, which have a fixed sequence and steps to undo, use a mediator.

Where the data lives. With each processor. A service keeps what it needs, often as a copy built from the events it has read, so an event has to carry enough for its readers to act on. At Quill the services still share one database; the two styles combine.

Strong and weak. Strong on fault tolerance, because a processor that is slow or down delays only its own work while the notices wait for it; on elasticity, because each processor is scaled by the length of its queue; on performance as the customer feels it; and on evolvability, since a new reader needs no change to the poster. Weak on simplicity and testability: the flow is written down nowhere, and it behaves differently depending on timing. Weak, too, wherever the business needs one immediate answer that everyone agrees on.

The cost of leaving. High, in both directions. Every reader has been written to expect things late and sometimes twice, and how a poster makes sure a notice really is posted is a chapter of its own, the Atlas's fifteenth. Turning such a flow back into calls, or calls into such a flow, means redesigning it.

Error handling is the part that most often goes missing. In a call, the caller is standing there when it fails. In an asynchronous flow the poster left long ago, so the failure needs somewhere to go. Each channel gets a path: retry a set number of times, then park the event where a person or a program will look, and post an event that says so. Quill's Dispatch tries a courier three times, then posts booking failed, and Ordering reacts by offering the next courier that can carry the parcel.

Sometimes a service that only has the noticeboard needs an answer. Request-reply over events does it: post the question with a reference and a return address, and wait for a notice bearing the same reference. It works, and it is a call with extra steps. The rule is that when the caller cannot continue without the answer, it should call. The exception is a responder that is slow or often absent, where waiting on a channel beats holding a connection open; the cost is time limits and matching references that a plain call gives you free.

Because the style looks like the assembly line with more arrows, the two are worth separating:

Pipeline Event-driven
Shape One line in a fixed order A web; any number of readers for each event
What moves The work itself, changed at each station Notices that something happened
The next step is known by The line Nobody, or the mediator
It ends At the consumer, with a result When nobody reacts any more

Order taking at Quill no longer waits for a courier. Bramble's loyalty system subscribed to order placed and the Ordering team changed nothing. Marcus was right about everything that happens after the order. Ingrid was right about the price, which is still a call, and about visibility: every event now carries the order's reference, and the list of who reads each event is kept beside its definition.

Remember it as: post what happened and let whoever cares act on it; when you need an answer now, ask directly instead.

◷How we got hereGregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf's Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003) gave messaging its vocabulary: channel,…

Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf's Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003) gave messaging its vocabulary: channel, publish and subscribe, request-reply, the correlation identifier, the dead letter channel. They were reacting to integration by remote procedure call, which made a network look like a function call and failed like a network. Mark Richards (2015) set out the two topologies, broker and mediator, used here. In 2017 Martin Fowler's "What do you mean by 'Event-Driven'?" separated the several things people had come to mean by the term, and Ben Stopford's Designing Event-Driven Systems (2018) argued for events as a system's backbone.

⚠The traps
  • Event-driven for a question that needs an answer: the sign is a request event, a reply event and a caller waiting between them with a time limit. It is a call rebuilt from notices, slower and harder to follow.
  • No error path: the sign is that nobody can say where an event goes after its last failed attempt. It is retried for ever or silently dropped, and either way an order is never dispatched and nobody is told.
  • The event with no owner: the sign is an event that two services both post, or one whose fields cannot be changed because nobody knows who reads them. Each notice needs one poster who owns its format.
  • The flow nobody can see: the sign is that answering "what happens after an order is placed?" means searching every repository for subscribers. Changes then have effects that nobody predicted.
◉Spot it

A design note from the basket team:

When a customer opens the basket, Ordering posts a PriceRequested event carrying the basket's reference. Pricing subscribes, works out the prices and posts PriceCalculated with the same reference. Ordering waits up to two seconds for that event and then shows the basket. An event that fails three times is parked for the pricing team. Each event has exactly one publisher.

Show the answer

Answer The basket cannot be shown without the prices, so this is a question that needs an answer, built out of two events and a wait. The sign is a caller blocked between a request event and a reply event. Everything else is sound: one publisher, a reference, an error path. The fix is for Ordering to call Pricing and keep events for what happens after the basket is shown.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Does the sender need the answer before it can carry on: yes or no?
  2. Where does this event go after its last failed attempt, and who looks there?
  3. Who is the one publisher of this event, and how many readers does it have today?

Still argued: whether events should be the default way for services to work together. Ben Stopford (2018) holds that services should share facts through a durable stream of events, each building from it whatever it needs, because that gives the loosest coupling and keeps the whole running when a part is down. This was Marcus's case. Martin Fowler (2017) holds that event notification makes it easy to build services that are nicely decoupled and a system whose overall flow can no longer be seen, debugged or safely changed, because that flow is stated nowhere. This was Ingrid's. The field has not chosen. Most systems that work use both, and the skill is in knowing which interaction is which.

What Ana learned

  • Call when the caller cannot continue without the answer, and post an event for everything that can happen afterwards.
  • Design where a failed event goes before the successful path ships.
  • Give each event one publisher, and keep the list of its readers where that publisher can see it.

…but

Lena has set the date for the first joint sale: Bramble's back-to-school week, with Quill's catalogue offered to two million Bramble customers. Kofi rehearsed it, with price and stock lookups at fifty times the normal rate for two hours. The database was on its knees within four minutes, and order entry, which shares it, went down as well.

Chapter 10 · Act IIIStalls That Carry Their Own Stock#

The problem

On an ordinary day Quill answers about forty price and stock lookups a second. Kofi's rehearsal of the joint sale sent two thousand requests a second for two hours, a quarter of them changes to a basket. The database begins to queue at about six hundred. Four minutes in, connections ran out, and order entry, which shares that database, stopped with it. Adding application servers changed nothing, because every one of them was waiting on the same database. The sale was three weeks away.

Ingrid proposed the familiar remedy: a read-only copy of the database and a cache in front of it. Marcus proposed taking the database out of the request path altogether, with the data held in memory beside the code.

Ana had both rehearsed. With Ingrid's design the lookups were served comfortably. The five hundred basket changes a second were not: each is a write, a cache does nothing for writes, and order entry still slowed to a crawl. With a prototype of Marcus's, the database saw a gentle, steady trickle and order entry did not notice the sale at all.

The idea

The space-based style is market stalls that each carry their own stock, and settle with the warehouse afterwards. Its one move is to remove the central database from the path of a request.

The parts. A processing unit is the application code together with an in-memory copy of the data it works on; there are many identical units, started and stopped as the load changes. An in-memory data grid keeps the units' copies in step by passing each change from one unit to the others. A data pump is a channel that carries changes away from the units. A data writer takes changes from the pump and writes them to the database. A data reader loads data from the database into a unit that is starting cold.

How they talk. A request goes to any unit and is answered from memory. A change is made in that unit's memory, copied to the other units by the grid, and sent down the pump. The database hears about it some seconds later, in batches.

Where the data lives. In memory, in every unit, and for the moment that is the working truth. The database is the long-term record, a little behind. It is what a cold unit is filled from and what the nightly line and the invoices read.

Strong and weak. Strong on elasticity and performance: add units, and each answers from its own memory with no shared queue. Fault tolerance is good on the request path, since losing a unit loses no data the others do not hold. It is weak on simplicity and testability, because the behaviour depends on load and on how fast copies converge, and neither is easy to reproduce. It is weak on cost: the working data is held in memory many times over. And it is wrong for data that must agree at every instant, because two units can change the same thing in the same second.

The cost of leaving. High. Code written against memory that the grid copies around is not code written against a database, and moving in either direction means rewriting how the application reads and writes.

It is often mistaken for something much cheaper:

A cache in front of a database Space-based
The database is In the path of every write and every miss Out of the request path
Memory holds Copies of some answers, which may be dropped The whole working set
A write goes To the database, then the cache is corrected To memory, then to the database later
The limit on load How fast the database can write Memory, and how fast units stay in step
If memory is lost Slower, still correct Refilled from the database, without what had not yet been pumped
Cost Low High

Caching and read copies belong to the system design book, chapters 9 and 5, and they are the first thing to try. Ingrid's premise was that the crowd would mostly be reading, and for a crowd that only reads she is right and the left-hand column is enough. This crowd also wrote five hundred times a second.

The rule that keeps the style safe is to put in the units only data that can be briefly out of step. A basket belongs to one customer, so two units rarely disagree about it, and a supplier's cost changes once a night. The last pallet of a sale item is different: two units can each sell it. So the stalls take lookups and baskets, and the moment of purchase, the stock decrement and the credit check, remains a call to Ordering against the database. That keeps the purchase correct, and it means checkout is the one step that cannot go faster than the database. The rule can be relaxed where a collision is rare and cheap to apologise for, a back-ordered box of pencils, and the apology is the cost.

The style has a relative. In the actor model, a program is many small actors, each with private state, that affect each other only by sending messages and share no memory at all. Platforms built on it reach the same end by the same instinct: keep state next to the code that uses it, and let nothing central sit in the path.

Remember it as: each stall sells from its own stock and settles with the warehouse later: fast for crowds, wrong for the last item on the shelf.

◷How we got hereDavid Gelernter's Linda language (1985) let parallel programs cooperate by placing items in a shared "tuple…

David Gelernter's Linda language (1985) let parallel programs cooperate by placing items in a shared "tuple space" and taking them out, instead of calling one another, and the style is named after that space. Carl Hewitt, Peter Bishop and Richard Steiger had proposed the actor model in 1973 with a similar aim, computation without shared state. Commercial in-memory data grids followed in the 2000s, for systems whose crowds arrive all at once and whose databases could not be made to keep up. Mark Richards (2015) described the arrangement as an architecture style in its own right, for systems with high and unpredictable numbers of simultaneous users, and rated it low for ease of development and of testing.

⚠The traps
  • Space-based for data that must agree: the sign is two units selling the same last item, or approving two orders against one credit limit, and a nightly job that "repairs collisions". Customers have already been told yes.
  • The grid as system of record: the sign is a data writer that is absent, or has been failing unnoticed. Memory is then the only copy, and a full restart loses the day.
  • Space-based for a steady load: the sign is a unit count that never changes. The system pays for elasticity it does not use, and a larger database server would have done.
◉Spot it
Show the answer

Answer Nothing carries changes back to the database: there is a reader and no pump or writer. The sign is that the only thing connected to the database is the reader. The grid has become the system of record, so the baskets exist only in memory, and a restart of all the units empties every one. The fix is a data pump and a data writer, and an alarm on how far the writer is behind.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What is the peak rate, how long does it last, and on how many days a year does it happen?
  2. Which data in the units could two units change in the same second, and is there a rule for which change wins: yes or no?
  3. If every unit stopped now, how many minutes of changes would be lost?

Still argued: whether to take the database out of the path or make the database go further. Mark Richards (2015) holds that for high and unpredictable concurrency the central database is the limit that no amount of application scaling removes, and that only moving the working data into memory removes it. This was Marcus's case. Nick Craver's account of Stack Overflow's architecture (2016) shows a very busy public site served from a handful of well-tuned database servers with a cache, and stands for the view that a relational database on good hardware goes far further than most teams assume, at a fraction of the complexity. This was Ingrid's. Each is right for a different load, so the argument is settled, case by case, by measuring the peak and counting its writes.

What Ana learned

  • Measure the peak and what it is made of before choosing, because copies can serve the reads and it is the writes that decide.
  • Put in the units only data that can be briefly out of step, and keep what must agree behind a call.
  • Check every day that the data writer is keeping up, because the database is still the record.

…but

The sale held. In October finance sent Ana the bill. The units had been scaled down after the sale, but the grid's minimum of eight and its licence are paid for all year round, for a peak that comes on six days. The same week, the team that converts uploaded order spreadsheets asked for four more servers, for a job that is busy from eight to ten on Monday mornings and close to idle the rest of the week.

Chapter 11 · Act IIIRenting by the Hour#

The problem

Six in ten of Quill's orders arrive as an uploaded spreadsheet, and a converter checks each one and turns it into an order. On a Monday about 500 arrive between eight and ten. For the rest of the week there are a few dozen an hour, and at night and at weekends there are none.

The converter runs on two servers. They are idle for most of the week and not enough for Monday, when the queue now lasts until noon. A primary school's order for the first day of term sat in that queue until 11:40, missed the dispatch cut-off and arrived a day late. The team asked for four more servers, which would also be idle for most of the week.

Finance had just queried the grid from the last chapter on the same grounds: money spent on machines that mostly wait.

Marcus proposed functions: code that the cloud provider runs when a file arrives and stops when it has finished, billed by the second. Ingrid had two objections. Every function is written against one provider's storage, queues and permissions, so leaving means rewriting. And a function that has not run for a while takes time to wake.

The idea

Serverless is renting the hall by the hour: no rent when it is empty, and a wait while the lights come on. The servers are the provider's, and you do not pay for them while your code is idle.

The parts. Functions and managed services. A function is a small piece of code that the provider starts on demand and stops when idle; this half is called function as a service. The other half is managed back-end services: file storage, queues, databases and sign-in that the provider operates and you only configure. Triggers join them: a file arrives, a message arrives, a request arrives.

How they talk. Through triggers and the managed services, almost always asynchronously. A file landing in storage starts one function; that function leaves a message on a queue; the message starts the next. Functions do not hold connections to each other.

Where the data lives. Never in a function, which remembers nothing from one run to the next. It lives in the managed stores.

Strong and weak. Strongest of any style on elasticity: from nothing to a thousand copies and back with nobody doing anything. Cost is good for work that comes in bursts. Deployability is good, since each function ships alone, and fault tolerance is good, since the provider restarts and retries. Performance is weak where a person is waiting, because of the cold start. Testability is weak, because the behaviour is mostly the provider's services and they do not run on a laptop. Simplicity is fair at best: each piece is trivial and the wiring between them is not.

The cost of leaving. The code inside a function moves easily. The triggers, permissions, queues and stores around it do not, and they are most of the system. That is lock-in, and it is a trade-off like any other: the price of leaving, multiplied by the chance of having to, against what the provider's services save every day. Avoiding it has a price too, usually a home-made layer that hides the provider and uses none of its services well.

A cold start is the wait while the lights come on. When a function has not run recently the provider must start a fresh copy, which takes from a few tenths of a second to several seconds. A spreadsheet conversion that runs for twenty seconds does not care. A customer pressing a button does. So the rule is to keep cold starts off any path a person waits on. Providers will keep copies warm for a fee, which is a legitimate way to break the rule, and it means paying rent on an empty hall, the thing the style was chosen to avoid.

The cost has a shape worth drawing on any whiteboard. Pay-per-use starts at nothing and rises in a straight line with use. A server is a flat line: the same whether busy or idle. The lines cross, and the crossover is the number to know. Kofi worked it out. At the prices Bramble pays, one conversion costs about a fortieth of a penny in function time, and a server costs £90 a month. Twelve thousand conversions a month come to about £3. The crossover is near 350,000 a month, one every eight seconds around the clock. The converter is far below it. Quill's price lookups, at forty a second all day, are far above it and have a person waiting, so they stay where they are.

Microservices Serverless functions
The unit A service: one capability, always running A function: one action, running only when triggered
You operate The service, its runtime and its scaling The code and its configuration
Kept between requests Connections, caches Nothing
Billed for Capacity, busy or idle Each run
Start-up delay When deployed Possibly on any request
Tied to A container platform, fairly portable One provider's triggers and services

The converter moved to a function, and so did invoice rendering at month end and the receivers for partners' notifications. On Monday every upload gets its own copy, and the queue is gone. Marcus was right about all three. Ingrid was right that they are now tied to the provider, so Ana had the cost of leaving estimated, at about two weeks for all of them, and wrote it beside the decision. Her premise, that the tie is too dear, would hold for a system that was large, central and likely to move.

Remember it as: rent by the hour what is usually idle, own what is always busy, and keep the wait for the lights off the critical path.

◷How we got hereAmazon announced AWS Lambda in November 2014: upload a function, name the event that should start it, and pay…

Amazon announced AWS Lambda in November 2014: upload a function, name the event that should start it, and pay for each request and for the time it runs. It answered a complaint as old as hosting, paying for servers that sit idle and employing people to look after them. The name serverless spread to cover the managed services such functions depend on, and Mike Roberts's long article "Serverless Architectures" (2016, revised 2018) fixed the definition used here, functions plus managed back-end services, and set out the drawbacks plainly, cold starts and dependence on one vendor among them. Criticism followed too: Joseph Hellerstein and colleagues (2019) argued that the first generation of functions suited only a narrow class of work, and Gregor Hohpe (2019) argued that avoiding lock-in has costs of its own, which are seldom counted.

⚠The traps
  • Function pinball: the sign is one action that bounces through eight functions and five queues, each trivial. Nobody can follow or test the path, and every bounce adds delay and cost.
  • Serverless for steady heavy load: the sign is a function that runs at a constant rate all day. Past the crossover it costs more than the server that would do the same work.
  • The cold start on the critical path: the sign is an occasional response of several seconds on something a customer is waiting for, most often first thing in the morning.
  • Lock-in ignored, and lock-in feared: the sign is either that nobody has estimated what leaving would cost, or that a home-made layer hides every provider service so that none is used well. In both cases the trade-off was never made.
◉Spot it

A design note from the order-entry team:

The postcode lookup on the new-account form becomes a function. It is called when a customer types a delivery postcode: about forty times a day, and almost never at night. It asks the address provider for the matching streets and returns them to the form. It will cost under £1 a month. Leaving the provider would mean rewriting its trigger and permissions, estimated at three days.

Show the answer

Answer A customer is waiting on this function, and at forty calls a day it is cold almost every time: the cold start is on the critical path. The sign is a step a person waits on, with long gaps between calls. The cost and the lock-in have been weighed properly. The fix is to keep the lookup inside the Ordering service, which is already running, or to pay for a warm copy and record that the saving has gone.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. How many times a month does this run, and where is the crossover with a server that is always on?
  2. Is a person waiting for this function to answer: yes or no?
  3. What would have to be rewritten to leave this provider, in days?

Still argued: how much lock-in matters. Gregor Hohpe (2019) holds that lock-in is not a yes-or-no property, that every way of avoiding it has its own cost in complexity and in provider features left unused, and that a team should accept it wherever the benefit outweighs the price of switching multiplied by the chance of having to. This was the case Marcus made. Joseph Hellerstein and colleagues (2019) hold that the first generation of functions restricts what can be built, with short-lived code that cannot address other code directly and must fetch all its data over the network, and that building within those limits commits a system to one provider's proprietary services. This was Ingrid's. Both describe real costs. Which is larger depends on how central the system is and how long it must live.

What Ana learned

  • Plot renting against owning before moving anything, and move what sits well below the crossover.
  • Keep whatever a customer waits for away from a cold start, or pay for a warm copy and say so.
  • Estimate the cost of leaving in days, and write it beside the decision.

…but

Encouraged, the upload team split the converter into eleven functions: one to unzip, one to detect the format, one for each validation rule, joined by seven queues. An upload that fails now fails somewhere among them, and nobody can say where. Marcus's draft goes the same way on principle, with nothing larger than could be rewritten in two weeks. It divides the Ordering service into fourteen.

Chapter 12 · Act IIIHow Small Is Small Enough?#

The problem

The eleven functions lasted three weeks. Then a school's upload vanished between two of them, and it took a day to find the queue it was sitting in.

Marcus's draft would do the same to the Ordering service, dividing it into fourteen: order capture, validation, credit check, amendment, cancellation and nine more. His case is that a small service is easy to understand, easy to hand to one team and easy to replace. Ingrid's case for keeping four services was that they work. One said "too big" and the other said "too many", and neither could say what size would be right.

There was already one piece of evidence. Last quarter a team had moved the credit check out of Ordering into a service of its own, with its own table of credit limits. Placing an order then meant two things had to happen in two places: Ordering saves the order, and Credit reduces what the account has left. One Friday afternoon the Credit service was slow. Orders were saved, the calls to reduce the limits timed out, and nothing tried again. Thirty-seven orders were accepted beyond their accounts' limits, and £61,000 of goods left the warehouse on credit that nobody had approved.

The service was small. It was easy to understand. It was the wrong size.

The idea

Granularity is how small a shop can be before the shopkeeper spends the day walking between shops. Size turns out to be a poor guide to it. What decides the right size is two sets of forces, and the question for any proposed split is which of them are present.

Disintegrators are reasons to pull a service apart:

  • Scope and function: it does two things that have nothing to do with each other.
  • Volatility: one part changes weekly and the rest once a year.
  • Scalability and throughput: one part needs many more copies than the rest.
  • Fault tolerance: one part's failures should not take the rest down.
  • Security: one part handles data that needs tighter access.
  • Extensibility: one part will grow by additions that are already planned.

Integrators are reasons to keep it together, or to put it back:

  • Database transactions: the parts must change data together, all or nothing.
  • Workflow: the parts would call each other on almost every request.
  • Shared code: they would share a body of code that changes with both.
  • Data relationships: their data is so interlinked that every query would cross the boundary.

The rule is that a split needs a disintegrator you can name and must survive all four integrators. The credit check had one of the first kind, scope, and ran straight into the strongest of the second: an order and the credit it uses up must change together. The rule can be broken. If the reason to split is strong enough, a transaction can be replaced by a saga, a sequence of separate steps with an undo for each, which the Atlas explains in chapter 16. The cost is that someone must then design what the database used to do for nothing.

That design has three choices in it: whether the services talk synchronously or asynchronously (communication), whether the whole must succeed or fail as one or may settle later (consistency), and whether one coordinator runs the steps or each service reacts to the last (coordination). Three choices of two make eight combinations, and the authors of Software Architecture: The Hard Parts gave each a name. This is the saga trade-off matrix:

Saga Communication Consistency Coordination What you get
Epic Synchronous Atomic Orchestrated Behaves like the old transaction; tightest coupling, slowest
Phone Tag Synchronous Atomic Choreographed All-or-nothing with nobody in charge; error handling is hard
Fairy Tale Synchronous Eventual Orchestrated A coordinator, each step committing alone; the usual sound choice
Time Travel Synchronous Eventual Choreographed A chain of calls; fine for simple one-way flows
Fantasy Fiction Asynchronous Atomic Orchestrated Atomic over messages; much complexity, little gain
Horror Story Asynchronous Atomic Choreographed The hardest of the eight; avoid
Parallel Asynchronous Eventual Orchestrated Scales well, and errors still have a home
Anthology Asynchronous Eventual Choreographed Loosest coupling and highest throughput; hardest to follow

The matrix is useful less for its names than because it shows there is a choice. The team that split out the credit check never made one. They wrote two synchronous calls, assumed both would succeed, and put nobody in charge of the case where one did not: a Phone Tag saga with the error handling left out.

Code that both halves need has three possible homes. A shared library is compiled into each service; it suits stable code and is chapter 4's trap for business rules that change. A shared service is one running copy that everyone calls; there is one place to change, and every caller is now down whenever it is. A sidecar is a small separate process deployed beside each service, carrying what every service needs and no business cares about: logging, security checks, traffic control. The working rule is to share operational code freely and business rules rarely; a small, stable value such as Money is the exception worth a library.

Follow the disintegrators all the way and you reach the microservices style: a street of small shops, each with its own till and stockroom. Each service is one business capability with its own data, its own build and release, and usually its own team, and the services deal with each other as equals by calls and events. It is the strongest style for deployability, elasticity, fault tolerance and evolvability, and among the weakest for simplicity and cost, because every integrator that was overridden has become a network call, a copy of data or a saga. Testing is only fair: each part is easy to test and the whole is not. The Atlas defines the style in its chapter 2 and prices it in chapter 21, and its row is in the next chapter's table.

Quill's credit check went back into Ordering, where an order and its credit change in one transaction. The eleven upload functions became three. Ingrid was right about thirteen of Marcus's fourteen. He was right about one: taking in uploaded orders changes weekly as customers' spreadsheets change, arrives in bursts, and hands over a finished order without sharing a transaction. It has two disintegrators and no integrator, and it stays outside Ordering, as the functions of chapter 11.

Remember it as: split a service only when a named force pulls it apart and no stronger force holds it together.

◷How we got hereAfter 2014 the commonest question about a service was how big it should be, and Sam Newman's Building…

After 2014 the commonest question about a service was how big it should be, and Sam Newman's Building Microservices (2015) passed on Jon Eaves's rule of thumb that a service should be small enough to rewrite in two weeks. Teams that took size as the goal produced the failure Mark Richards named grains of sand in 2016: services so fine that the system was mostly network. Neal Ford, Mark Richards, Pramod Sadalage and Zhamak Dehghani reacted to that in Software Architecture: The Hard Parts (2021), which is the source of this chapter's forces. They replaced the question of size with disintegrators and integrators, and set out the eight sagas so that a team dividing a transaction would know it was choosing.

⚠The traps
  • Grains of sand: the sign is a single request that crosses five services, and a team of four that owns twenty. More time goes on the network than on the work.
  • Splitting for its own sake: the sign is a split justified by "smaller is better" or "single responsibility", with no disintegrator named. The cost arrives and no benefit was ever specified.
  • Ignoring the integrators: the sign is two services that are always deployed together, or a transaction across two services described as "reliable enough with retries". They are one service with a network through the middle.
  • The saga chosen by accident: the sign is that nobody can say whether a flow across services is meant to be all-or-nothing or to settle later, or who notices a failed step. The choice was made by whoever wrote the first call.
◉Spot it

A proposal from the pricing team:

Split Pricing into two services, Price Lookup and Contract Terms. Contract Terms changes most weeks; Price Lookup has not changed in a year, so they should deploy separately. Each gets its own schema, and no transaction spans the two. On every lookup, Price Lookup will call Contract Terms to fetch the account's discount band.

Show the answer

Answer The two halves would talk on every single request, which is the workflow integrator. The sign is the phrase "on every lookup". The disintegrator is real and named, volatility, and there is no shared transaction. But every price would now depend on a second service being up and fast. The fix is to keep them together, or to let Price Lookup hold its own copy of the discount bands, brought up to date by an event when terms change.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Which named force justifies this split: scope, volatility, scale, fault tolerance, security or extensibility?
  2. Do the two parts ever need to change data together, all or nothing?
  3. On an ordinary request, how many times will the two parts call each other?

Still argued: whether size is a guide at all. Jon Eaves's rule of thumb, reported by Sam Newman (2015) as one that suited its author's context, is a service small enough to be rewritten in two weeks. On that view small services are easier to understand, to give to one team and to throw away, and a size limit keeps them so. This was Marcus's case. Ford, Richards, Sadalage and Dehghani (2021) hold that size is a result and not a target, and that each boundary should be justified by a force. A service may properly be large when integrators hold it together. This was Ingrid's. Recent practice leans towards forces. Size rules survive as a prompt to look, which is a fair use of them.

What Ana learned

  • Ask for the named force behind every proposed split, and test it against the four that hold things together.
  • Keep in one service whatever must change in one transaction, unless you are prepared to design the saga on purpose.
  • Share operational code freely and business rules rarely.

…but

Marcus's final report arrived on the Friday, and its recommendation fitted on one page: a single target architecture for the whole merged company, event-driven microservices on one platform, for order entry, the nightly line, the hall and the storefront alike. Lena liked that it fitted on one slide. She asked Ana for her objection, on one slide as well.

Chapter 13 · Act IVNot One Plan for the Whole Town#

The problem

Marcus's target architecture was one diagram with the word all in its title: event-driven microservices on a single platform, for every system in both companies. His argument was a serious one. One style means one set of skills to hire for, one platform to run, and engineers who can move between teams without relearning their trade.

Ana could not answer that with a preference, and did not have to. Lena wanted evidence before the board met, so Marcus's team rebuilt one system "to the standard" as a proof of concept: the nightly line of chapter 6. Fourteen stations became six services passing nine million events through the broker. It ran beside the old line for three weeks, and Kofi kept the figures. It took over six hours where the line takes four, and cost four times as much to run. Re-running a night meant replaying the events and took most of a day. On the second Monday it missed six o'clock. The pilot was switched off and the line was kept.

The idea

Choosing a style is zoning: a factory, a school and a row of houses do not share one plan. The choice starts from the system's three driving characteristics, never from a style.

The first question is monolithic or distributed. If every part of the system needs the same things, the system is one quantum, and a monolithic style will be cheaper, simpler and easier to test. If some part must scale, deploy or fail separately from the rest, there is more than one quantum, and the network is a price worth paying. From this follows the rule that Marcus's slide broke: choose one style per quantum, not one per company. A company's systems have different drivers, and a style that serves one set will fail another.

The tree gives candidates. The comparison table shortlists among them, and the trade-off session of chapter 3 decides. For cost, Good means cheap.

Style Deployability Elasticity Fault tolerance Performance Simplicity Testability Evolvability Cost
Layered Poor: every change ships everything Poor: scales only as a whole Poor: one process, one failure Fair: in-process calls, one database Good: one program, familiar to everyone Fair: layers stubbed, changes cross them Poor: business changes cross every layer Good: one build, one thing running
Modular monolith Poor: one release for every module Poor: scales only as a whole Poor: one process, one failure Fair: in-process calls, one database Good: one program, enforced borders Good: a module tests alone Good: business change stays in module Good: one build, one thing running
Pipeline Poor: the whole line ships together Poor: stations scale together Fair: restartable only if designed Fair: sequential, suits batches Good: one direction, one contract Good: file in, file out Good: add or swap a station Good: cheap to build and run
Microkernel Fair: stalls can ship without core Poor: everything under one roof Poor: a bad plug-in hurts all Fair: in-process calls through contract Good: small core, uniform plug-ins Good: plug-in tested against contract Good: add a plug-in, touch nothing Good: one deployable to run
Service-based Good: each team ships alone Fair: coarse services, shared database Fair: services isolated, database shared Fair: few network hops Fair: simplest of the distributed styles Good: one business area per service Good: cut along business lines Fair: few services, data unmoved
Event-driven Good: processors ship alone Good: scale each by queue length Good: notices wait for slow readers Good: nobody waits for anybody Poor: the flow is written nowhere Poor: behaviour depends on timing Good: new reader, poster unchanged Fair: a broker and its upkeep
Space-based Fair: many identical units, one grid Good: add units, no shared queue Good: every unit holds a copy Good: answers come from memory Poor: replication, pumps and collisions Poor: needs load to reproduce Fair: code is built around grid Poor: data in memory many times
Serverless Good: each function ships alone Good: zero to thousands, unattended Good: provider restarts and retries Poor: cold starts, limits per run Fair: trivial pieces, intricate wiring Poor: provider's services not on laptops Fair: tied to one provider's services Good: nothing while idle; watch crossover
Microservices Good: every service ships alone Good: scale one capability alone Good: failures stay in one service Fair: every interaction is a hop Poor: sagas, contracts, many moving parts Fair: parts easy, the whole hard Good: small parts replaced independently Poor: a build and pager each

These ratings are this book's judgement, taken from chapters 5 to 12 where those chapters speak and reasoned the same way where they are silent. They follow the star ratings in Richards and Ford (2020) in their broad pattern: monolithic styles are cheap and simple, distributed ones elastic and costly. They differ in using three levels where that book uses five, and in adding the modular monolith and serverless, which its 2020 catalogue does not rate.

Read the pilot against the table. The nightly line must finish by six, be re-runnable and be cheap to change. The pipeline row is good on simplicity, testability and cost. The event-driven and microservices rows are good on elasticity and deployability, which the line does not need, and poor on simplicity, which it does.

Styles also combine, and a hybrid is normal. Quill's back office is service-based, its services talk by events, the nightly line beside it is a pipeline, Dispatch contains a hall, and order intake is rented by the hour. The rule is one style for each quantum at the top level, with others nested inside where a part has a different shape. Its limit is the one Marcus named: each style in use is another thing to staff and to run, so a hybrid should be chosen and never drift into being.

That is also where his argument holds. Standardising on one style is the right call when a company's systems have much the same drivers, when it is small enough that one platform is all it can operate, or when people move between teams so often that familiarity is worth more than fit. And one layer should be standard everywhere: the platform beneath the systems, how they are deployed, observed and secured. Standardise the roads. The buildings follow what each must survive.

Remember it as: zone the town: choose each system's style from what that system must survive, and standardise the roads, not the buildings.

◷How we got hereRoy Fielding's dissertation in 2000 supplied the reasoning for choosing among styles.

Roy Fielding's dissertation in 2000 supplied the reasoning for choosing among styles. He defined a style as a named, coordinated set of constraints, each adopted to induce a property the system needs, and derived the web's own style by adding constraints one at a time. That was a reaction to styles chosen by fashion or by analogy. Mark Richards and Neal Ford's Fundamentals of Software Architecture (2020) turned the reasoning into a working tool: one catalogue of the common styles, each rated against the same characteristics, so that a choice could begin from the drivers. The case for a company-wide standard has its own literature, and Ross, Weill and Robertson's Enterprise Architecture as Strategy (2006) is the argument Marcus was making. The golden hammer, below, comes from the same 1998 catalogue of antipatterns as chapter 3's analysis paralysis.

⚠The traps
  • One style for the whole company: the sign is a target architecture with one diagram and the word "all". Systems with opposite drivers are forced into one shape, and at least one of them fails its own scenario.
  • The golden hammer: the sign is the style of the architect's last success proposed for a new system before its drivers have been named. The reasons are found afterwards.
  • Distributed without a reason: the sign is several deployables and nobody able to say which part must scale, deploy or fail separately. The network's costs are paid and nothing was bought with them.
  • The style the team cannot run: the sign is a design that needs a broker, a grid or a cloud service that nobody on the team has operated, with no line in the plan for learning it. It is learned in production.
◉Spot it

From a target architecture for finance reporting:

Month-end reports are produced once a month by one team of three. Drivers: correct figures, low running cost, quick to change when the accountants ask. Proposed style: eight microservices, one for each family of reports, each with its own database, on the standard platform, so that reporting matches the rest of the estate.

Show the answer

Answer The style is distributed without a reason. The drivers are correctness, cost and ease of change; nothing here must scale, deploy or fail separately, and one team of three owns all of it. The sign is that nobody can say which part needs to be separate; the only reason offered is conformity. The fix is a monolithic style, here a modular monolith or a pipeline, on the standard platform.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Which three driving characteristics does this style serve, and which cells of the table say so?
  2. Which part of this system must scale, deploy or fail separately from the rest?
  3. Who on the team has run this style in production before?

Still argued: one standard style for a company, or a style for each system. Ross, Weill and Robertson (2006) hold that a company should choose how far to standardise its processes and technology, and that those which standardise deliberately build a foundation that makes later projects cheaper and faster. Variety, on this view, is a cost paid for ever in skills, tools and operations. Richards and Ford (2020), following Fielding (2000), hold that each style buys some characteristics by giving up others, so that one style across systems with different drivers gives every system the wrong trade somewhere. Fit, on this view, is what an architecture is for. Many organisations now split the difference by level, with a standard platform and a style chosen per system, but where that line belongs is still disputed.

What Ana learned

  • Start every choice of style from the system's three drivers, and ask first whether all of its parts need the same things.
  • Use the table to shortlist and the trade-off session to decide.
  • Standardise the platform and the way of working, and let each system's shape follow its drivers.

…but

Three weeks after the styles were agreed, a new engineering manager, hired from a company that ran on microservices, asked in a planning meeting why Quill's back office shares one database "against best practice", and proposed dividing it. Ingrid was on holiday. Nobody else in the room could remember the argument well enough to answer him.

Chapter 14 · Act IVWrite It Down#

The problem

The decision to keep one database behind the back-office services was made in chapter 8, by four people in a room, after an afternoon's argument. It was a good decision, and it left no trace.

So when the new engineering manager asked why, nobody could tell him. Ingrid was away. Ana remembered the conclusion and not the reasoning. His proposal sounded sensible, and a team began giving Invoicing a database of its own. Two weeks in, they reached month-end reconciliation, the one query that joins orders, invoices, payments and credit notes, and stopped. Three people's fortnight was written off and the work was reversed.

Then came the meeting about the reversal. Ingrid was back. For ninety minutes she, Marcus, the manager and Ana had the argument of chapter 8 again, from the beginning, and reached the same conclusion. It was the third time the decision had been made, and afterwards there was still nothing to show for it but four people's memories.

Marcus's remedy was a proper architecture document: every view of the system and every decision, in one maintained volume. Ingrid's was the opposite. She had never needed a document. The decisions were in the code, and she was there to explain them.

The idea

An architecture decision record, ADR for short, is the planning file: what was decided, when, what was known, and what it cost. It is one decision on about one page, in plain text, numbered, and kept in the repository beside the code it governs. It has five parts.

  • Title: the decision as a short phrase.
  • Status: proposed, accepted, or superseded, with dates.
  • Context: what was true and what mattered when the decision was made. This is the part memory loses first.
  • Decision: one or two sentences beginning "We will".
  • Consequences: what becomes easier and what becomes harder. A record that names no cost has not finished thinking.

Bramble adds a sixth line, Review when: the evidence that would reopen the decision.

Here is the record that should have existed in chapter 8:

ADR 7: The back-office services share one database

Status: Accepted, 26 June. Superseded in part by ADR 19.

Context: Three teams could not ship separately from one release. The failing characteristic was deployability, not scale or resilience. The database has 400 tables. Month-end reconciliation is one query across orders, invoices, payments and credit notes, and finance must be able to reproduce any invoice to the penny.

Decision: We will split the back office into four services (Ordering, Pricing, Invoicing, Dispatch) and keep one database, with a schema for each service and exactly one service writing to each schema. Reads across schemas are allowed by agreement and are listed in this repository.

Consequences: Each team ships on its own day. Reconciliation and reporting stay as single queries. Harder: a column that another service reads cannot be renamed without that service. All four services slow down or fail together if the database does. No service can be scaled or secured separately at the level of its data.

Review when: a service needs its own scaling or its own security boundary; or schema changes force more than one service to deploy more than twice in a quarter.

With that in the repository, the manager's question takes two minutes: read ADR 7. His proposal is still welcome, but it now has a form. It is a new record, and its context must say what has changed since the old one.

Something did change, in the new year. Lena's third request was to offer Quill's invoicing to Bramble's marketplace sellers, so that they could invoice their own business customers through it.

ADR 19: Invoicing gets its own database

Status: Accepted, 13 January. Supersedes ADR 7 for the Invoicing service only.

Context: Invoicing will be offered to Bramble's marketplace sellers. Their invoices belong to other companies and must be kept apart from Quill's data, and volume is expected to rise twentyfold. Both are review triggers named in ADR 7. Nothing has changed for Ordering, Pricing or Dispatch.

Decision: We will move the invoicing schema to a database owned by the Invoicing service. Month-end reconciliation will read invoices from a copy that Invoicing publishes each night.

Consequences: Invoicing can be secured and scaled alone. Harder: reconciliation now depends on a nightly copy and is up to a day behind. Orders and invoices can no longer change in one transaction, so "mark as invoiced" becomes an event. There is one more database to run and back up.

Review when: reconciliation needs figures less than a day old; or the sellers' volume stays under a tenth of the forecast for two quarters.

This is superseding, and it is the only way an accepted record changes. ADR 7's text is left exactly as it was written; only its status line gains a pointer to its successor. The reason is that the old record is still true as history: it says what was known in June. The rule has an obvious limit: a typing error may be corrected. It also has a cost: a reader must follow the chain, which is why the pointers run both ways.

The records in number order are the decision log. A rejected proposal stays in it, because "we considered that in March, and here is why not" is half of what the log is for.

Not every decision earns a record. The test is chapter 1's: would reversing it take more than one team and one month? A log with a page for every library choice hides its walls among its furniture.

Two other documents are often confused with the record, and a large decision may properly have all three.

Decision record Design document Request for comments
Answers What did we decide, and why? How will we build it? What do you think of this proposal?
Written When the decision is made Before building Before deciding
Length About a page Many pages Any
Afterwards Never edited, only superseded Stale once the thing is built Closed; its outcome becomes a decision record
Kept With the code, for good With the project Wherever the discussion was held

Ingrid was right that Marcus's volume would not have been read; large documents are not, and they are out of date within a quarter. His premise, that someone will keep it current, holds where documentation is a contractual deliverable, as in regulated or safety-critical work. Marcus was right that a decision held in one head is not recorded. Ingrid's premise, that she is there to explain, holds for a team small enough to ask her and a system she never leaves. It failed for the length of one holiday and cost three people a fortnight.

Remember it as: one page for each decision: what we decided, what we knew, what it costs, and what would make us think again.

◷How we got hereArchitecture documents of the 1990s and 2000s ran to hundreds of pages, and Michael Nygard's "Documenting…

Architecture documents of the 1990s and 2000s ran to hundreds of pages, and Michael Nygard's "Documenting Architecture Decisions" (2011) began from the observation that nobody reads them or keeps them current. What gets lost, he argued, is the motivation behind each decision, so that newcomers must either accept a decision blindly or change it blindly. His answer was the short record used in this chapter, kept with the code and superseded, never rewritten. Heavier templates existed already, among them Jeff Tyree and Art Akerman's in 2005, but it was the one-page form that spread. Richards and Ford (2020) named the three failures that a decision log prevents, which head the list below: covering your assets, Groundhog Day and email-driven architecture.

⚠The traps
  • Covering your assets: the sign is a decision postponed again "until we know more", or a record that lists options and chooses none. Teams decide for themselves in the gap, differently.
  • Groundhog Day: the sign is the same decision reopened in three meetings because nobody can find why it was made. Each meeting costs an afternoon and ends where the first did.
  • Email-driven architecture: the sign is a decision that exists only in an email thread or a chat channel. Whoever was not copied, or joined later, never learns of it and cannot search for it.
  • The record written afterwards and never superseded: the sign is a record dated months after the code, tidier than the decision ever was, or an accepted record that the system now contradicts. A log that is not true is worse than no log, because people trust it.
◉Spot it
ADR 22: Stock events are published through the company broker

Status: Accepted, 2 February.

Context: Three other teams need to know when stock arrives. The warehouse system was calling each of them in turn, and a slow receiver held up the goods-in screen.

Decision: We will publish "stock received" from the warehouse system to the broker. Other teams subscribe.

Consequences: The warehouse system no longer needs to know its readers. A slow reader cannot hold up goods-in. A new reader needs no change to the warehouse system.
Show the answer

Answer The consequences are all benefits. The decision is a sound one, but it has costs the record does not admit: what happens after a delivery can no longer be read in one place, readers must cope with late and repeated events, and there is a broker to run. The sign is a consequences section with nothing that is harder. The fix is to add those lines, so that the next reader knows they were seen and accepted.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Where is the record of this decision, and what is its number?
  2. What does the record say became harder?
  3. Which sentence of the record's context is no longer true?

Still argued: how much architecture documentation is enough. Paul Clements and his co-authors (2002) hold that an architecture must be documented as a set of views with the reasoning behind them, because the people who most need it were not in the room. This was Marcus's volume. The Agile Manifesto (2001) values working software over comprehensive documentation, and teams in that tradition rely on the code and on conversation to carry what matters. This was Ingrid's position. Nygard's record (2011) was designed to sit between them, and it has been widely adopted as the minimum. How much more than the minimum a system needs is still argued, and regulated industries answer differently from start-ups.

What Ana learned

  • Write one page for each decision that fails the reversal test, on the day it is made, and keep it beside the code.
  • Refuse to accept a record whose consequences name nothing that became harder.
  • Reopen a decision only with a new record that says what has changed.

…but

The log now holds nineteen records. A developer who joined in January read ADR 7 and asked which box "the back office" was. Three teams sent her three diagrams. One had four boxes, one had nineteen, and one had a cylinder labelled "Quill". At the meeting to settle it, two people argued about an arrow for ten minutes before finding that one of them meant a service by a box and the other meant a class.

Chapter 15 · Act IVDraw It So They Can Read It#

The problem

Each of the three diagrams was accurate, to the person who drew it. The four-box one showed the services. The nineteen-box one showed services, modules and two database tables, all as rectangles. The cylinder labelled "Quill" was how the storefront team thought of the whole thing. None of them said what a box stood for, what an arrow meant, or how far away the viewer was standing.

The new developer had picked the nineteen-box diagram, because it had the most detail. On it was a box called Reconciliation, with arrows in and out, looking like every other box. She spent three weeks building an integration that called it. Reconciliation is a module inside the Invoicing service. It cannot be called from anywhere. Her work was thrown away.

Marcus's answer was a standard. There is a formal notation with defined meanings for every shape and line, taught for decades; adopt it and a diagram means the same to everyone trained to read it. Ingrid's answer was that she had run Quill for eleven years on whiteboard sketches, drawn in conversation and wiped afterwards, and that formal models are out of date before they are finished.

The idea

The C4 model is a set of map scales: the region, the town, the building, the room. Nobody tries to show a country and a floor plan on one sheet. C4 gives software four sheets, each answering a different question for a different reader.

Level Shows A box is Drawn for
Context The system, its users and the systems around it A whole system Everyone, including people who do not write code
Container What runs inside the system and how the pieces talk Something separately runnable: a service, an application, a database, a queue Whoever builds or operates it
Component The parts inside one container A module with one job The team that owns that container
Code Classes inside one component A class or a function Almost nobody; generate it when needed

"Container" is C4's word for anything that runs or stores data on its own, and has nothing to do with any packaging technology of the same name.

Here is the Quill back office at the first three scales. The context diagram is the one to show Lena.

Zoom in on that one box and it becomes the container diagram, which is the one the new developer needed.

Zoom in once more, on Ordering alone, and the Ordering team has its component diagram.

The levels are half of the model. The other half is four notation rules, and they are the rules this book's diagrams have followed since chapter 1; go back and check.

  1. State the level. Each structure diagram has a caption that begins with it.
  2. Label every arrow with a verb, and between containers with the protocol or medium. An unlabelled line says only that two things are somehow related.
  3. One level of abstraction on one diagram. A class never stands beside a service.
  4. Give a legend. Say what each shape, colour and line style means. In this book a solid arrow is a call that waits for its answer, a dashed arrow is asynchronous, and a frame around several boxes is one deployable; the full key is in the epilogue.

The rules have a limit. A sketch on a whiteboard in the middle of a conversation needs none of them, because its author is standing beside it answering questions. They apply from the moment a diagram is saved where someone can find it without its author. Skipping them then costs what it cost here: three weeks of one person's work.

How a diagram is kept matters as much as how it is drawn. Every diagram in this book is a few lines of text, stored beside the chapter that uses it and changed in the same commit. That is diagrams as code: the diagram is reviewed in the same pull request as the change it describes, its history can be read, and nobody needs a drawing tool that only one colleague owns. It does not make a diagram true, which is the next chapter's subject, but it removes the usual reasons for letting one go stale.

C4 is not the only way to organise views, and two others are worth knowing by name. Philippe Kruchten's 4+1 model describes a system through four views (logical, process, development and physical) tied together by a fifth, a handful of scenarios. arc42 is a template for a whole architecture document, in which diagrams like these fill some of the sections.

Bramble now keeps a context and a container diagram for every system, as text, beside its decision log, and a component diagram only where a team wants one. Marcus was right that a notation must have agreed meanings. His premise, that a formal standard is the way to get them, holds where models are exchanged between companies or used to generate code; it fails where most readers were never taught the standard. Ingrid was right that a sketch is enough while its author is in the room, and the new developer is what happens when she is not.

Remember it as: draw one scale at a time, say which, label every arrow and give the key; a map without a scale is only a picture.

◷How we got herePhilippe Kruchten's "4+1" paper (1995) made the first widely accepted case that no single diagram can…

Philippe Kruchten's "4+1" paper (1995) made the first widely accepted case that no single diagram can describe a system, reacting to drawings that tried to show structure, processes and hardware at once. The Unified Modeling Language, adopted as a standard in 1997, then gave the industry a rich formal notation, and through the 2000s most teams quietly stopped using it, leaving diagrams of unexplained boxes and lines. Gernot Starke and Peter Hruschka's arc42 template dates from 2005. Simon Brown's C4 model was a reaction to both extremes: it grew out of his teaching between about 2006 and 2009, and has carried the name since 2011. It asks for very little: a few levels, any notation, and enough labelling that a stranger can read the result.

⚠The traps
  • Boxes and lines with no legend: the sign is a diagram on which only the author can say what a box, a colour or a dashed line means. Every reader invents a meaning, and they differ.
  • Mixed levels of abstraction: the sign is a class or a table drawn beside a service, in the same shape. A reader cannot tell what can be deployed or called, and builds against something that cannot.
  • One diagram for every audience: the sign is a single wall-sized drawing shown to the board and to the engineer on call. It is too detailed for the first and too vague for the second.
  • Diagram rot: the sign is a diagram older than the last three releases, in a tool one person has. It is trusted for exactly as long as it takes to mislead someone.
◉Spot it
Show the answer

Answer PriceCalculator is a class, drawn on a container diagram as if it were something that runs on its own: two levels of abstraction are mixed. The sign is one box whose name is a code identifier among boxes named for services. A reader would conclude that the calculator can be deployed, scaled or called over the network. The fix is to remove it, let the arrow to the database start from the Pricing service, and show the calculator, if anyone needs it, on Pricing's component diagram.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What level is this diagram, and what does one box on it stand for?
  2. What does this arrow mean: who calls whom, by what protocol, and does the caller wait?
  3. When was this diagram last changed, and is it changed in the same pull request as the code: yes or no?

Still argued: a formal standard notation, or light diagrams with a legend. The case the Object Management Group made in adopting the Unified Modeling Language (1997) is that a standard with defined meanings lets any trained reader understand any diagram and lets tools check it. Home-made boxes mean only what their author intended. This was Marcus's proposal. Martin Fowler (2003) argued that the valuable use of such notation is the selective sketch that helps people talk. Complete formal models, on his account, cost more to keep true than they return. This was Ingrid's practice. Brown's C4 keeps the sketch's lightness and adds just enough rule to survive its author's absence. Everyday practice has moved that way, while formal modelling keeps its place in fields where diagrams are contracts.

What Ana learned

  • Draw a context and a container diagram for every system, state the level and label every arrow.
  • Keep diagrams as text beside the code, so that they are reviewed and changed with it.
  • Give each audience the scale it can use, and stop drawing at the scale nobody reads.

…but

The records and the diagrams now agree, and both are in the repository. Two weeks later an ordinary pull request in Ordering added a query that reads Invoicing's tables directly, to save a call. Two reviewers approved it. The container diagram still shows no such arrow.

Chapter 16 · Act IVKeep It True#

The problem

The order history screen needed to show whether each order had been invoiced. The developer had two proper ways to find out: the copy that Ordering builds from Invoicing's events, which runs a few seconds behind, or a call to the Invoicing service. A third way was quicker. Invoicing's own data-access classes were still within Ordering's reach, left over from before the split, and an old configuration file still held a password for Invoicing's database. The screen could simply use them to read the invoice table.

The pull request was forty lines. The tests passed. Two reviewers approved it, and neither had ADR 19 in mind.

Ten days later the Invoicing team renamed a column, in their own database, for the sellers' launch. At 09:20 on a Tuesday the order history screen began to fail for every customer, and it stayed down for fifty minutes while the Invoicing team tried to understand how a change that touched nobody else's code had broken somebody else's screen.

The rule existed. It was written in a record and drawn on a diagram. Nobody had broken it on purpose. It depended on every reviewer remembering it on every pull request, and on one ordinary afternoon they did not.

Marcus drew the larger conclusion: an old system patched this way will keep doing this, so build the target clean and retire what is there. Ingrid drew the opposite one: nobody who rewrites a working system from nothing gets back what they threw away.

The idea

A fitness function is the building inspection, repeated on every change. It is any automated check that reports whether the system still has a characteristic it was designed for, or still obeys a rule it was designed around. Two distinctions sort them:

  • Atomic or holistic. An atomic check looks at one thing in isolation: Ordering uses no other service's internals. A holistic one looks at several things together, usually on a running system: with the nightly line running, order entry still answers within a second.
  • Triggered or continual. A triggered check runs when something happens: a commit, a build, a deployment. A continual one runs all the time in production: how far the data writer of chapter 10 has fallen behind.

The cheapest and most useful kind is atomic and triggered: an architecture test in the build. It reads the code's own dependencies and fails if a forbidden one exists.

public final class ServiceBoundaryCheck {
    public record Dependency(String fromClass, String toClass) {}

    /** Fails the build if a service uses another service's internals. */
    public static void check(String service, List<Dependency> dependencies) {
        String own = "quill." + service + ".";
        var violations = dependencies.stream()
            .filter(d -> d.fromClass().startsWith(own))
            .filter(d -> !d.toClass().startsWith(own))
            .filter(d -> d.toClass().contains(".internal."))
            .toList();
        if (!violations.isEmpty())
            throw new AssertionError(service
                + " reaches into another service's internals, against ADR 19: "
                + violations);
    }
}

The list of dependencies comes from a tool that reads the compiled classes. Architecture-test libraries that do this exist for every major language and run inside the ordinary unit-test run, so a violation stops the same build a failing test would, with a message that names the record. The developer of the order history screen would have met ADR 19 on a laptop, in the first minute.

Better than detecting the wrong thing is making it impossible. Each service's database account now sees only its own data, so the forbidden query fails wherever it is run. Permissions are fitness functions too, of the continual kind.

A fitness function looks like a test and is a different thing:

Test Fitness function
Protects What the system does A characteristic or a structural rule
Fails when A feature is wrong The architecture has moved
Written from A requirement A decision record or a scenario
Example An order over its credit limit is refused Ordering uses nothing inside Invoicing; the nightly run ends by 06:00
Runs In the build In the build, at deployment, or continually in production

The rule is that every architectural rule gets a check, and the record says which. Its limit is the rule that cannot be checked cheaply by a machine, such as "every reader of this event is listed". That one becomes a named person's review on a set date, and it will decay faster than the automated kind, which is the cost.

What the checks hold back has two names. Erosion is the breaking of a stated rule, as the pull request did.
