Drift is the extension nobody applied for: change that breaks no rule, because nobody thought to make one, and still moves the system away from its design. The reports that bypassed the business layer in chapter 5 were drift.

Shortcuts taken along the way are technical debt: deferred maintenance, with interest. In Martin Fowler's terms (2009) it is deliberate when the team knows it is borrowing, as in "read the table directly for this release, and replace it by March", and inadvertent when nobody knew, which is the usual case and the worse one. Deliberate debt is a legitimate tool if it is written in a register with what it costs each month and what will trigger repayment. The forbidden query was debt that nobody knew they owed.

With records, diagrams and checks in place, an architecture can be changed in small steps without losing its shape, and that is evolutionary architecture: leaving the gable wall plain because a wing will be added there. Here the town stops being a good guide, and the book should say so. A building cannot be rebuilt every week. Software can be copied, replaced and rebuilt cheaply and repeatedly, and that difference is the whole case for evolving a system under inspection instead of planning it once like a cathedral, or demolishing it and starting again.

The same visibility is wanted for technology choices, and the usual instrument is a technology radar: a short published list, revised a few times a year, sorting each technology into adopt, trial, assess or hold. On Bramble's, the message broker is adopt, the data grid is trial, and reading another service's database is hold.

Ingrid was right about the back office. It is being repaired where it stands, one check at a time, and the fifteen years of pricing rules in it are not being rediscovered the hard way. Marcus was right about a smaller thing: the first upload converter was thrown away and rebuilt as functions, and nobody mourned it. His premise, that replacing is cheaper than repairing, holds for a system small enough to rewrite in weeks and understood well enough to rewrite correctly.

Remember it as: a rule that nothing checks is a wish; put the inspection in the build, and it happens on every change.

◷How we got hereWard Cunningham introduced the debt metaphor in 1992, to explain to his boss why code shipped in a hurry had…

Ward Cunningham introduced the debt metaphor in 1992, to explain to his boss why code shipped in a hurry had to be reworked: a little debt speeds delivery, provided it is repaid. The same year Perry and Wolf gave erosion and drift their names. For two decades the usual defence against both was a review board and a document, and neither could keep pace once teams began releasing every day. ThoughtWorks published its first Technology Radar in 2010, making one firm's technology judgements public and regular. Then Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons and Patrick Kua's Building Evolutionary Architectures (2017) borrowed the term fitness function from evolutionary computing and proposed that architectural characteristics be protected the way behaviour already was, by automated checks in the delivery pipeline. The categories used above are theirs.

⚠The traps
  • The rule on the wiki: the sign is an architectural rule that exists as a sentence in a document and nowhere in the build. It is kept until the first busy week.
  • The failing check everyone ignores: the sign is a check that has been red, or set to "warn only", for a month. The rule is now optional, and so, by example, is every check beside it.
  • Debt with no register: the sign is "we'll fix it later" with no list, no owner and no date. Nobody can say how much is owed or what it costs, so it is never the right time to repay.
  • The big-bang re-architecture: the sign is a plan to stop other work and rebuild everything on the target, delivering nothing until the end. The old system keeps changing meanwhile, and the new one chases it.
◉Spot it
public static void check(List<Dependency> dependencies) {
    var violations = dependencies.stream()
        .filter(d -> d.fromClass().startsWith("quill.ordering."))
        .filter(d -> d.toClass().startsWith("quill.invoicing.internal."))
        .toList();
    if (!violations.isEmpty())
        System.out.println("WARNING: against ADR 19: " + violations);
}
Show the answer

Answer The check prints a warning and returns normally, so the build passes whatever it finds. The sign is a fitness function that cannot fail. Within a month the warning is one line among thousands in a build log that nobody reads. The fix is to throw, so that the build stops.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Which check fails the build if this rule is broken, and which decision record does its message name?
  2. Which checks are red or set to warn today, and since when?
  3. What is on the debt register, and what does its largest item cost each month?

Still argued: repair or replace. Joel Spolsky (2000) holds that rewriting a working system from scratch is the worst strategic mistake a software company can make, because the old code's ugliness is years of fixes for real problems, and a rewrite discards them and spends years getting back to where it started. This was Ingrid's position. Martin Fowler (2014) holds that the best code a team can write today may be code it should expect to throw away in a few years, and that designing a system to be replaced as needs outgrow it is a sound strategy and not a failure. This was Marcus's. Evolutionary architecture is an attempt to make the question smaller: replace parts continually, under checks, so that the whole is never rewritten and never frozen.

What Ana learned

  • Give every rule in a decision record a check that fails the build, and name the record in its message.
  • Treat a red check as a stopped line, and delete any check you are not prepared to obey.
  • Keep a register of debt with its monthly cost, and repay it in small steps under the checks.

…but

Forty-one checks now run on every change, and they are green. But every exception to one, every new record and every "are we allowed to?" comes to Ana. Her review calendar is full for three weeks ahead. A team that needed a queue waited eleven days for her approval, then added it without telling her.

Chapter 17 · Act IVThe Architect in the Room#

The problem

Every exception to a check, every new decision record and every question that begins "are we allowed to" now goes to Ana. There are nine teams. Her reviews are booked three weeks ahead.

One team needed a queue between two of its own components. It asked for approval, waited eleven days, and then added the queue without telling her. Nobody was told, so nobody watched it. Three weeks later it filled overnight, and two thousand dispatch notifications sat in it until morning.

A second incident bothered her more. A team proposed the cloud provider's managed queue, and Ana said no, because in 2019 she had lost messages on a managed queue and spent a weekend finding them. The team's engineer showed her, politely, that it had been a different product with a different guarantee, six years ago. She had not built anything on either since.

Ingrid recognised the first problem and not the second. For eleven years she had made every significant decision at Quill herself, and the system had one mind behind it, which showed in its consistency. But Quill had twelve developers, and she had written code alongside them every week.

The idea

The architect is the town planner, who walks the streets and also sits in the council meeting. The earlier chapters were about decisions. This one is about how decisions get made, which is itself a set of decisions, with trade-offs like any other.

Breadth over depth. What anyone knows falls into three parts: what they know well, what they know exists, and what they have never heard of. A developer is valued for the first, depth. An architect is valued for the second, breadth: knowing that five ways of doing something exist, and when each one fits, is worth more to a decision than mastery of one. Nobody can keep depth in everything, and an architect who tries ends up defending expertise that has gone stale, which is what Ana did with the queue. The rule has a limit. With no depth at all, an architect cannot judge what things cost, so most keep their hands in somewhere, and pay for it in time.

The architect elevator. A large organisation is a tall building: strategy is set in the penthouse and systems are built in the engine room, and the floors between speak different languages. The architect's distinctive work is riding the elevator: telling Lena what "one company within a year" costs in release trains and databases, and telling the teams why invoicing for sellers matters enough to split one off. An architect who stays on the top floor produces slides, and one who stays at the bottom is a senior developer with a grander title.

How much control. There is no fixed right amount. Richards and Ford (2020) list what it depends on: how well the team's members know each other, the team's size, its experience, the complexity of the work and how long it will last. A large, newly formed team on a long and complicated project needs an architect close by and firm. A small team that has worked together for years needs to be left alone. The same architect should behave differently in the two rooms, and should loosen the grip as a team learns.

The architecture advice process. This replaces approval. It is one rule with one condition: anyone may take an architectural decision, provided that before deciding they seek advice from everyone the decision will meaningfully affect and from people with expertise in the matter. In the town: anyone may build, after asking the neighbours and the planner, and filing the plan. They are not obliged to follow the advice. They are obliged to seek it, to write down what they were told, and to record the decision, in the form of chapter 14. A weekly advisory forum, an hour long and open to all, is where proposals are aired and where everyone hears the advice given to everyone else.

The architect is in this picture as an adviser, one voice among those with expertise, and no arrow in it is labelled "approves". That is the change. The rule has a limit as well: a one-way door that binds every team, such as the choice of platform or the security baseline, keeps a named owner, and is slower for it.

Principles and the paved road. People deciding for themselves need to know what the organisation cares about. A short list of principles says so, each drawn from a decision already in the log: every table has one writing service; a customer never waits on a courier. And a paved road makes the right way the easy way: a supported platform, and project templates with the fitness functions already wired in. A team that stays on the road needs nobody's advice. A team that leaves it must seek advice, and say why in a record.

Under the new arrangement the team with the queue would have decided within two days, with operations in the conversation and an alarm on the queue. Ana's calendar emptied. She now spends one day a week working inside a team, a different one each month, which is where a planner learns what the streets are like.

Ingrid's way was right for Quill as it was. One mind can hold a system built by twelve people, and the consistency that results is real. It stops working when the one mind becomes the queue. What survives of it is the list of principles, which is conceptual integrity written down so that nine teams can share it.

Remember it as: anyone may decide, after asking those affected and those who know, and writing it down; the architect advises and keeps the roads paved.

◷How we got hereFred Brooks argued in 1975 that a system's conceptual integrity depends on its design coming from one mind,…

Fred Brooks argued in 1975 that a system's conceptual integrity depends on its design coming from one mind, or very few, and for decades the architect was that mind: a role above the teams, approving their designs. Agile teams of the 2000s distrusted the role, and Martin Fowler's 2003 column (chapter 1) already contrasted the architect who makes all the decisions with the one who works beside the team. Gregor Hohpe's elevator, an article in 2017 and a book, The Software Architect Elevator, in 2020, described what the role is for in a large organisation. Andrew Harmel-Law's "Scaling the Practice of Architecture, Conversationally" (2021) set out the advice process, the forum and the supporting records and principles, reacting to architects who had become queues; he has said in an interview that the advice process comes from Frederic Laloux's writing on self-managing organisations. The paved road was Netflix's phrase by 2016, and Richards and Ford (2020) named the frozen caveman.

⚠The traps
  • The ivory tower: the sign is decisions that arrive as documents from people who have not been in a team's code, or on call, this year. The decisions ignore what things cost, and the teams quietly work around them.
  • The architect as bottleneck: the sign is a queue for architectural approval measured in weeks. Teams either wait or stop asking, and both are worse than a slightly wrong decision made on time.
  • The frozen caveman: the sign is an architect who raises the same objection to every proposal, from one bad experience years ago, about technology that has since changed. Good options are refused for reasons that no longer apply.
  • Control where guidance would do: the sign is an experienced team required to seek permission for choices it could reverse in a day. It stops thinking for itself, or its best people leave.
◉Spot it

A draft of the new decision process:

Any team may take an architectural decision. Before deciding, the team asks for advice from the teams affected and from people with relevant expertise, and presents the proposal at the weekly forum. The decision, and the advice received, are written up as a decision record. The record takes effect once the head of architecture has approved it.

Show the answer

Answer The last sentence puts approval back, so every decision still waits on one person: the bottleneck with extra steps. The sign is the word "approved" in a process described as advice. The fix is for the record to take effect when the deciding team accepts it. The architect's view is recorded in it as advice, like anyone else's, and a disagreement is left visible there.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Who took this decision, whose advice did they seek, and where is that written?
  2. How many days did this team wait for an architectural answer last quarter?
  3. When did the person advising on this technology last build or run something with it?

Still argued: one deciding mind, or decisions spread among the teams. Fred Brooks (1975) holds that conceptual integrity is the most important property a system can have, and that it comes only from a design held in one mind or a very few. It is worth restricting who may decide in order to get it. This was Ingrid's practice. Andrew Harmel-Law (2021) holds that in an organisation of many teams no central decider has the context or the hours, and that decisions are best taken by the people who will live with them once they have sought advice. Coherence then comes from shared principles and open conversation. Each describes an organisation of a particular size, and the dispute is over where one becomes the other.

What Ana learned

  • Stop approving and start advising: let teams decide once they have sought advice, and insist on the record.
  • Publish the principles and pave the road, so that the easy way is the right way and needs no meeting.
  • Spend the time this frees inside the teams, because advice from someone who has built nothing lately is the caveman's.

…but

Lena has booked the board review for March, a year to the week after the acquisition. She wants to be shown the architecture of the whole company, and she would still like it on one slide.

Chapter 18 · Act IVOne Town, Three Plans#

The problem

The board meets in March, a year to the week after Bramble bought Quill, and Lena has to tell it what the company's architecture is and why it should go on paying for it.

She has two slides to choose from. Marcus's is the one from chapter 13: one style, one diagram, the word all. It is easy to present. Ana's has three rows on it, which looks, at a glance, like three times the trouble.

The board will also ask about the year's three most expensive weeks, because finance has itemised them. A pilot migration that was built, run for three weeks and switched off. A database split that was started, found to break month-end and reversed. Fifty minutes with no order history, caused by a pull request that two people approved. Lena wants to be able to say that these will not happen again, and why.

Ana noticed what the three had in common. The pilot was a style chosen without the system's drivers. The split was a decision reopened without its record. The outage was a rule without a check. Each was a different missing piece of the same practice.

The idea

An architecture review is that practice, done in public for a whole system or a whole company. It is a fixed list of questions, asked of every proposal, including the reviewer's own:

  1. What are the systems, meaning the parts with different needs?
  2. For each, what are its three driving characteristics, as scenarios with numbers?
  3. Which style serves them, and what does that style give up?
  4. Where is each significant decision recorded?
  5. Which check keeps each rule true?
  6. What evidence would trigger a review of each decision?

A review that skips the second question is a discussion of taste. One that skips the sixth produces decisions that are either never looked at again or reopened whenever someone new dislikes them. The rule is that every recorded decision names its trigger. A two-way door does not need one, since it can simply be changed, and writing triggers for furniture is the same waste as writing records for it.

This is Ana's slide.

System Must survive Style Gives up
The nightly line Finished by six; safe to re-run; every invoice reproducible Pipeline Prices that change within the day
The back office Each team ships alone; orders and credit correct; cheap to run Service-based, with events after the order Separate scaling; one database is one fate
The sale-day storefront Thousands of requests a second, on six days a year Space-based, with checkout as a call Simplicity and money; baskets briefly out of step

Two smaller pieces complete the picture: the partner integrations, a hall with stalls inside the back office's Dispatch service, and the intake of uploaded orders, rented by the hour. Under all of it is one platform, one message broker and one paved road.

At the rehearsal, Ana asked the questions this book has been collecting, of her own rows first, with Marcus and Ingrid in the room.

From chapter 6, of the nightly line: "If station seven fails at 03:10, which stations run again, and what is written twice?" Station seven and those after it; nothing, because each replaces its own output.

From chapter 13, of the back office: "Which part of this system must scale, deploy or fail separately from the rest?" Invoicing, since the sellers arrived, and ADR 19 has already given it its own database. Nothing else.

From chapter 10, of the storefront: "What is the peak rate, how long does it last, and on how many days a year does it happen?" Two thousand a second, for two hours, on six days. Ana said plainly that this is the most expensive row and the decision she is least sure of.

From chapter 3, of the same row: "Which part of this decision could we undo in a week, and which part could we never undo?" The units can be switched off in a day. The basket code written for them would have to be rewritten.

From chapter 2, of Marcus's slide: "Which three characteristics decided this design, and which one did you give up to get them?" He answered without hedging. One set of skills, one way to operate, people who can move between teams. Those are the company's needs and belong to no single system, and what the design gives up is fit. He then made the point that settled the meeting: those three are exactly what a platform is for. His standard was adopted for the roads: one platform, one broker, one way to deploy and observe, and one event format between systems. He was right about the system that joins the systems.

Ingrid's question was her own. How many things is the company now running that nobody in it had run two years ago? A broker, a data grid and rented functions: three. She was right about order entry, the nightly batch and the shared database, and her question put a limit on the next year: no fourth.

Then the review recorded one decision in full. It was the oldest one.

ADR 31: Prices are fixed nightly; quotes are worked out on request and stored

Status: Accepted, 14 March. Records a decision first taken twelve years ago and never written down, as amended last May.

Context: Suppliers send price lists once a day. Contracts promise that a morning's price holds all day. Finance and the auditors must be able to reproduce any invoice to the penny for seven years. Since the acquisition, account managers must also be able to change a contract price during the day.

Decision: We will keep the nightly line as the only writer of the price table, and keep each night's table for seven years. During the day a quote is worked out on request by the same pricing component, and the quoted price is stored on the order line. Invoices use the order line's price.

Consequences: Any invoice can be reproduced from its order lines and that night's table. A contract change is in force within five minutes. Harder: a supplier's price change still waits for the night. A price is worked out in two places, the line and the request path, and they must agree to the penny. Nine million rows are recomputed every night whether or not they changed.

Fitness functions: the build fails if anything but the nightly line writes to the price table. Every night one account in a hundred is priced by both paths, and any difference raises an alarm.

Review when: suppliers send prices more than once a day; or more than one order in ten carries a same-day price change; or the nightly line finishes after 05:30 three times in a quarter.

From chapter 1: "Is the original reason for this decision still true today, yes or no, and how do you know?" Two of the three are, Ingrid said, and the record now says which. From chapter 14: "What does the record say became harder?" Three things, in its own words. From chapter 16: "Which check fails the build if this rule is broken, and which decision record does its message name?" The price-table check, and it names ADR 31.

Lena took the three-row slide to the board. Ingrid wrote ADR 31 herself. It took her twenty minutes, and it was the first decision record she had ever written.

Remember it as: for each system, three drivers, one style, the loss you accepted, the check that keeps it true, and the evidence that would reopen it.

◷How we got hereArchitecture reviews are older than most of this book's ideas.

Architecture reviews are older than most of this book's ideas. Large telecommunications companies ran them as a formal practice for years, and Joseph Maranzano and his colleagues described that experience in 2005; the trade-off method of chapter 3 gave such reviews scenarios to test against. What reviews usually produced, though, was a target: one end state for everything, with a plan to reach it, in the tradition of enterprise frameworks such as TOGAF (1995). Two reactions shaped this chapter. Dan McKinley's "Choose Boring Technology" (2015) argued that every new technology a company adopts has a lasting cost in attention, and that a company can afford only a few, about three "innovation tokens"; it is Ingrid's question in print. And Ford, Parsons and Kua (2017) argued that no end state can be known in advance, so an architecture should be steered and never finished.

⚠The traps
  • The uniform target architecture: the sign is a target-state diagram that is the same for every system, with a migration plan measured in years. Systems are then judged by their distance from the target and not by their own scenarios.
  • A review with no characteristics: the sign is a review that discusses boxes, products and standards and never asks what the system must survive. Its conclusions are the taste of the most senior person present.
  • A decision with no trigger for review: the sign is a record that names no evidence that would reopen it. It is then reopened by fashion, or never, and both are expensive.
◉Spot it

Minutes of the review of the partner hall:

Drivers confirmed: a new partner live within a day; a failing partner must not stop dispatch; running cost under £200 a month. Style: microkernel, with plug-ins written by partners run in a separate process. Loss accepted: plug-ins written in-house share one release. Recorded as ADR 27. Check: the build fails if the core names a plug-in. Next review: none planned.

Show the answer

Answer The decision has no trigger for review. Everything else is in order: drivers, a style that serves them, a stated loss, a record and a check. The sign is "none planned". Nobody will know when the hall has been outgrown, for instance when partners need to release their own stalls weekly. The fix is one line naming the evidence, such as "review when in-house plug-ins block each other's release twice in a quarter, or a partner's plug-in stops the core".

✎At the whiteboard
  1. How many systems does this plan cover, and does each have three drivers, a style and a stated loss: yes or no?
  2. Which decision here has no record, no check or no trigger?
  3. How many technologies does this plan add that nobody in the company has run for two years?

Still argued: whether a company should have a target architecture at all. The enterprise-architecture tradition, of which TOGAF (1995) is the best known, holds that an organisation should describe where its systems are, define the target state, and plan the transition, because without an agreed destination every project optimises for itself. This was the form of Marcus's report. Ford, Parsons and Kua (2017) hold that the business and its technology change faster than any multi-year plan, so that a target is out of date before it is reached. The workable alternative, on their account, is continual small change guided by automated checks. The board got something from each: a standard for the roads, and for the buildings a set of triggers in place of a destination.

What Ana learned

  • Review a company as a set of systems, each with its own three drivers, its style and its stated loss.
  • Standardise what the systems stand on, and count every new technology as money spent.
  • Give every recorded decision a check and a trigger, and when a trigger fires, decide again without embarrassment.

…but

There is no next crack, only the next trigger. In June the suppliers' trade body announced that price lists will be issued twice a day from next year. ADR 31 names that. Ingrid has put the review in the calendar. The epilogue is the plan of the town, for when your own triggers fire.

EpilogueThe Town Plan#

The reference: everything here appeared in the story.

The metaphor table

The town fails in one place, on purpose: a building cannot be rebuilt every week and software can, which is why chapter 16 leaves the metaphor behind.

The review checklist

Every trap in the book, with its tell-tale sign, for use in a review.

Foundations: act I (chapters 1–4)

  • Accidental architecture (ch. 1, The Decision Nobody Remembered Making): a constraint everyone works around and nobody can date or explain, described as "it has always done that".
  • Architecture as a phase (ch. 1, The Decision Nobody Remembered Making): an architecture document dated before the first commit and not edited since.
  • The framework mistaken for the architecture (ch. 1, The Decision Nobody Remembered Making): the sentence "our architecture is Spring Boot, PostgreSQL and Kafka".
  • Every characteristic a priority (ch. 2, What Must This Building Survive?): a list of ten or more qualities all marked high, or the words "these are all non-negotiable".
  • The unmeasurable characteristic (ch. 2, What Must This Building Survive?): an adjective with no number: "highly available", "fast", "scalable".
  • The forgotten implicit characteristic (ch. 2, What Must This Building Survive?): a quality so obvious to the people who run the system that it is on no list, such as "finished before the warehouse opens".
  • The generic architecture (ch. 2, What Must This Building Survive?): a design justified as "scalable, secure and resilient" that would suit any company equally.
  • Best practice without context (ch. 3, Nothing Is Free): a justification that ends at "it's best practice" with no scenario attached.
  • Analysis paralysis (ch. 3, Nothing Is Free): a third workshop about a choice that could be reversed in a week.
  • The one-way door walked through casually (ch. 3, Nothing Is Free): "we can always change it later" said of a data format, a published interface or a record being retired.
  • The two-way door decided by committee (ch. 3, Nothing Is Free): a steering group scheduled to choose a library or name a queue.
  • Benefits listed without costs (ch. 3, Nothing Is Free): a proposal with a gains column only, and silence when someone asks what it makes harder.
  • Copying a famous company (ch. 3, Nothing Is Free): a justification that names a firm a thousand times your size.
  • The shared library as hidden coupling (ch. 4, What Belongs Together): a common or utils library that holds a business rule and is compiled into several programs.
  • The entity trap (ch. 4, What Belongs Together): components named after tables, such as Customer Manager, Order Manager and Product Manager, each offering create, read, update and delete.
  • Dynamic connascence across a network (ch. 4, What Belongs Together): two services that only work when called in a certain order or within a certain time, with a wiki page as the only record.
  • Technical partitioning for domain change (ch. 4, What Belongs Together): every business change touches every layer and needs the screen team, the services team and the database team in one meeting.

One building: act II (chapters 5–7)

  • The sinkhole (ch. 5, The Terrace): a chain of methods with the same name in each layer, each calling the next and adding nothing.
  • The accidentally open layer (ch. 5, The Terrace): a query in a screen or a report that reads tables directly, with no record of anyone deciding it.
  • Lasagne (ch. 5, The Terrace): seven or eight thin layers, with facades, managers and mappers between the usual three, so that adding one field edits a file in each.
  • Layered by default (ch. 5, The Terrace): nobody can say why the system is layered except that the project template was.
  • Filters that share state (ch. 6, The Assembly Line): a static field, a shared working table or a running total that two stations both touch.
  • The filter that does everything (ch. 6, The Assembly Line): one station called "process" with six jobs and a thousand lines.
  • The pipeline with no re-run story (ch. 6, The Assembly Line): nobody can say, for a failure at station seven at 03:10, which stations run again and what would be written twice.
  • Plug-ins that depend on each other (ch. 7, The Hall and Its Stalls): a plug-in that imports another, or only works if another is loaded first.
  • The fat core (ch. 7, The Hall and Its Stalls): a plug-in's name in the core, as in if (courier.id().equals("northline")).
  • The unversioned contract (ch. 7, The Hall and Its Stalls): a contract changed in place with every plug-in rebuilt the same night.
  • A plug-in with access to the core's database (ch. 7, The Hall and Its Stalls): a connection or a repository handed to a plug-in "for convenience".

Many buildings: act III (chapters 8–12)

  • The shared schema that ripples (ch. 8, A Handful of Big Buildings): a column rename that needs four services deployed on the same night, or a table nobody can name the owner of.
  • The service bus returns (ch. 8, A Handful of Big Buildings): a "gateway" or "integration layer" between the screens and the services that has begun to make decisions of its own.
  • Service creep (ch. 8, A Handful of Big Buildings): a service count that goes from five to twenty in a year, each split sensible on its own, all still on one database.
  • Event-driven for a question that needs an answer (ch. 9, The Noticeboard): a request event, a reply event and a caller waiting between them with a time limit.
  • No error path (ch. 9, The Noticeboard): nobody can say where an event goes after its last failed attempt.
  • The event with no owner (ch. 9, The Noticeboard): an event that two services both post, or one whose fields cannot be changed because nobody knows who reads them.
  • The flow nobody can see (ch. 9, The Noticeboard): answering "what happens after an order is placed?" means searching every repository for subscribers.
  • Space-based for data that must agree (ch. 10, Stalls That Carry Their Own Stock): two units selling the same last item, or approving two orders against one credit limit, and a nightly job that "repairs collisions".
  • The grid as system of record (ch. 10, Stalls That Carry Their Own Stock): a data writer that is absent, or has been failing unnoticed.
  • Space-based for a steady load (ch. 10, Stalls That Carry Their Own Stock): a unit count that never changes.
  • Function pinball (ch. 11, Renting by the Hour): one action that bounces through eight functions and five queues, each trivial.
  • Serverless for steady heavy load (ch. 11, Renting by the Hour): a function that runs at a constant rate all day.
  • The cold start on the critical path (ch. 11, Renting by the Hour): an occasional response of several seconds on something a customer is waiting for, most often first thing in the morning.
  • Lock-in ignored, and lock-in feared (ch. 11, Renting by the Hour): either that nobody has estimated what leaving would cost, or that a home-made layer hides every provider service so that none is used well.
  • Grains of sand (ch. 12, How Small Is Small Enough?): a single request that crosses five services, and a team of four that owns twenty.
  • Splitting for its own sake (ch. 12, How Small Is Small Enough?): a split justified by "smaller is better" or "single responsibility", with no disintegrator named.
  • Ignoring the integrators (ch. 12, How Small Is Small Enough?): two services that are always deployed together, or a transaction across two services described as "reliable enough with retries".
  • The saga chosen by accident (ch. 12, How Small Is Small Enough?): nobody can say whether a flow across services is meant to be all-or-nothing or to settle later, or who notices a failed step.

Choosing and keeping: act IV (chapters 13–18)

  • One style for the whole company (ch. 13, Not One Plan for the Whole Town): a target architecture with one diagram and the word "all".
  • The golden hammer (ch. 13, Not One Plan for the Whole Town): the style of the architect's last success proposed for a new system before its drivers have been named.
  • Distributed without a reason (ch. 13, Not One Plan for the Whole Town): several deployables and nobody able to say which part must scale, deploy or fail separately.
  • The style the team cannot run (ch. 13, Not One Plan for the Whole Town): a design that needs a broker, a grid or a cloud service that nobody on the team has operated, with no line in the plan for learning it.
  • Covering your assets (ch. 14, Write It Down): a decision postponed again "until we know more", or a record that lists options and chooses none.
  • Groundhog Day (ch. 14, Write It Down): the same decision reopened in three meetings because nobody can find why it was made.
  • Email-driven architecture (ch. 14, Write It Down): a decision that exists only in an email thread or a chat channel.
  • The record written afterwards and never superseded (ch. 14, Write It Down): a record dated months after the code, tidier than the decision ever was, or an accepted record that the system now contradicts.
  • Boxes and lines with no legend (ch. 15, Draw It So They Can Read It): a diagram on which only the author can say what a box, a colour or a dashed line means.
  • Mixed levels of abstraction (ch. 15, Draw It So They Can Read It): a class or a table drawn beside a service, in the same shape.
  • One diagram for every audience (ch. 15, Draw It So They Can Read It): a single wall-sized drawing shown to the board and to the engineer on call.
  • Diagram rot (ch. 15, Draw It So They Can Read It): a diagram older than the last three releases, in a tool one person has.
  • The rule on the wiki (ch. 16, Keep It True): an architectural rule that exists as a sentence in a document and nowhere in the build.
  • The failing check everyone ignores (ch. 16, Keep It True): a check that has been red, or set to "warn only", for a month.
  • Debt with no register (ch. 16, Keep It True): "we'll fix it later" with no list, no owner and no date.
  • The big-bang re-architecture (ch. 16, Keep It True): a plan to stop other work and rebuild everything on the target, delivering nothing until the end.
  • The ivory tower (ch. 17, The Architect in the Room): decisions that arrive as documents from people who have not been in a team's code, or on call, this year.
  • The architect as bottleneck (ch. 17, The Architect in the Room): a queue for architectural approval measured in weeks.
  • The frozen caveman (ch. 17, The Architect in the Room): an architect who raises the same objection to every proposal, from one bad experience years ago, about technology that has since changed.
  • Control where guidance would do (ch. 17, The Architect in the Room): an experienced team required to seek permission for choices it could reverse in a day.
  • The uniform target architecture (ch. 18, One Town, Three Plans): a target-state diagram that is the same for every system, with a migration plan measured in years.
  • A review with no characteristics (ch. 18, One Town, Three Plans): a review that discusses boxes, products and standards and never asks what the system must survive.
  • A decision with no trigger for review (ch. 18, One Town, Three Plans): a record that names no evidence that would reopen it.

The style comparison table

Chapter 13's table, unchanged. For cost, Good means cheap.

Style Deployability Elasticity Fault tolerance Performance Simplicity Testability Evolvability Cost
Layered Poor: every change ships everything Poor: scales only as a whole Poor: one process, one failure Fair: in-process calls, one database Good: one program, familiar to everyone Fair: layers stubbed, changes cross them Poor: business changes cross every layer Good: one build, one thing running

Two templates

A quality-attribute scenario (chapter 2):

Scenario: <the characteristic, as an event someone could watch>

Source:
<Who or what causes it>

Stimulus:
<What they do, or what happens>

Environment:
<The conditions at the time: normal load, peak, during the nightly run>

Response:
<What the system does>

Measure:
<The number and the frequency that say it passed>

A decision record (chapter 14):

ADR <number>: <the decision, as a short phrase>

Status:
<Proposed, Accepted or Superseded, with the date and the record it supersedes or is superseded by>

Context:
<What was true and what mattered on the day: drivers, constraints, numbers>

Decision:
<One or two sentences beginning "We will">

Consequences:
<What becomes easier, and at least one thing that becomes harder>

Review when:
<The evidence that would reopen this decision>

Once the rule has a check, add a line Fitness functions: naming it, as ADR 31 does in chapter 18.

The diagram legend

The four notation rules of chapter 15: state the level under every structure diagram; label every arrow with a verb, and between containers with a protocol or medium; keep one level of abstraction on a diagram; and give a legend. This book's legend is the colours above, plus three conventions: a frame around several boxes is one deployable, a solid arrow is a call that waits, and a dashed arrow is asynchronous.

The timeline

To 1999: the vocabulary. Structure came first: layers, modules, pipes, coupling and cohesion. In the 1990s architecture became a subject with a definition, a catalogue of styles and the claim that qualities drive structure.

2000 to 2014: the practice. Reviews gained scenarios and trade-off points, decisions gained a deferral rule and then a one-page record, diagrams gained scales, and the service bus rose and fell.

2015 onward: the judgement. The styles were catalogued and rated, granularity got forces in place of sizes, and governance moved from review boards to checks in the build and advice between teams.

The reading list, by year

These are the milestones above. The sources behind each Still argued block are in research/milestones.md, with the date and the claim each was checked for.

  • 1964 Doug McIlroy, Bell Labs memorandum on connecting programs.
  • 1968 Edsger Dijkstra, "The Structure of the 'THE'-Multiprogramming System".
  • 1972 David Parnas, "On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules".
  • 1973 Carl Hewitt, Peter Bishop and Richard Steiger, "A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence".
  • 1974 Wayne Stevens, Glenford Myers and Larry Constantine, "Structured Design".
  • 1985 David Gelernter, "Generative Communication in Linda".
  • 1992 Dewayne Perry and Alexander Wolf, "Foundations for the Study of Software Architecture". Meilir Page-Jones, "Comparing Techniques by Means of Encapsulation and Connascence". Ward Cunningham, "The WyCash Portfolio Management System".
  • 1993 David Garlan and Mary Shaw, "An Introduction to Software Architecture".
  • 1995 Philippe Kruchten, "The 4+1 View Model of Architecture".
  • 1996 Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad and Stal, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture, Volume 1.
  • 1998 Len Bass, Paul Clements and Rick Kazman, Software Architecture in Practice. Read the scenario chapter in a later edition.
  • 2000 Rick Kazman, Mark Klein and Paul Clements, ATAM: Method for Architecture Evaluation. Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures.
  • 2003 Martin Fowler, "Who Needs an Architect?". Mary and Tom Poppendieck, Lean Software Development. Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns.
  • 2005 Thomas Erl, Service-Oriented Architecture: Concepts, Technology, and Design.
  • 2010 ThoughtWorks, Technology Radar, first edition.
  • 2011 ISO/IEC 25010. Michael Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions". Simon Brown, the C4 model (c4model.com).
  • 2014 AWS Lambda, announced in November.
  • 2015 Mark Richards, Software Architecture Patterns. Neal Ford and Mark Richards, Service-Based Architectures (video). Dan McKinley, "Choose Boring Technology".
  • 2016 Jeff Bezos, letter to shareholders for 2015. Mike Roberts, "Serverless Architectures" (revised 2018).
  • 2017 Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons and Patrick Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures.
  • 2020 Mark Richards and Neal Ford, Fundamentals of Software Architecture. If you read one more book, read this one. Gregor Hohpe, The Software Architect Elevator.
  • 2021 Neal Ford, Mark Richards, Pramod Sadalage and Zhamak Dehghani, Software Architecture: The Hard Parts. Andrew Harmel-Law, "Scaling the Practice of Architecture, Conversationally".
  • 2024 Vlad Khononov, Balancing Coupling in Software Design.

For where to draw the borders inside a system, read DDD and Microservices: The Atlas. For data, scale and staying up, read System Design: The Depot.
